title: Ant and bee colonies, and how insects pollinate flowers and recycle waste

summary.text: Without insects, many of the foods in your kitchen would not grow, and dead things would pile up. How do insects do this work? In this lesson you will find which foods needed an insect, test whether hairy or smooth carriers move more pollen, and time ants clearing crumbs.
summary.art: A bunch of tiny pale mango flowers with a honeybee and a shiny green fly on it, and below the tree a line of ants carrying a dead moth.

intro.hook: A bee lands on a pumpkin flower, drinks and flies away. Some weeks later a pumpkin hangs where that flower was. The bee came for a drink. So how did her visit make a pumpkin?
intro.text: The bee is hairy, and yellow pollen from the flower stuck to her hairs. At the next pumpkin flower, some of that pollen rubbed off. A flower needs pollen from another flower before seeds and a fruit can grow. The bee was collecting food for her colony, which is her family of thousands of sisters. In this lesson you find out how a colony lives. You test why a hairy body carries pollen so well. You also watch another kind of insect work: ants clearing crumbs from your floor.
intro.art: A honeybee dusted with yellow pollen climbing out of a large yellow pumpkin flower on a vine.

outcomes: I can say who lives in an ant colony or a bee colony, and what each member does.
I can explain how a new colony begins, and why a colony lives longer than its workers.
I can explain what pollination is, using the words pollen, anther and stigma.
I can test fairly whether a hairy or a smooth carrier moves more pollen, and say what my results show.
I can explain why insects visit flowers, and how flowers draw them.
I can name pollinators other than honeybees, and say which foods need insect pollinators.
I can explain how ants, flies, beetles and termites recycle dead things and waste.
I can say what harms insect pollinators and recyclers, and name one thing my family can do.

terms.meaning: One of the two thin feelers on an insect's head. An insect smells and touches with them.
terms.example: Two ants meet on a wall and touch antennae, to find out whether they belong to the same colony.
terms.art: The head of an ant with two long thin feelers, labelled antennae.

terms.meaning: An insect who lives in a large family that shares one nest and shares the work.
terms.example: Ants, honeybees and termites are social insects. A housefly lives alone.
terms.art: A honeybee comb crowded with bees on the left, and one housefly alone on a wall on the right.

terms.meaning: One family of social insects living in one nest. It can hold a few dozen members or many thousands.
terms.example: All the ants walking in one line on your kitchen wall belong to one colony.
terms.art: A cut-away view of an ant nest in soil with tunnels, chambers and many ants.

terms.meaning: The mother of the colony. She lays the eggs.
terms.example: A honeybee queen can lay more than 1,000 eggs in one day.
terms.art: A long-bodied queen honeybee on a comb with smaller worker bees in a ring around her.

terms.meaning: A daughter of the queen who does the work of the colony and usually has no young of her own.
terms.example: The ants you see carrying crumbs are all workers, and all of them are sisters.
terms.art: Three worker ants, one carrying a crumb, one carrying a white larva and one touching another ant with her antennae.

terms.meaning: The young of an insect after the egg hatches. A larva looks like a small soft grub and must be fed.
terms.example: Worker bees feed each larva in her wax cell many times a day.
terms.art: A honeybee comb seen close, with a white curled larva in the bottom of each open cell.

terms.meaning: A sweet liquid that flowers make. Insects drink it for energy.
terms.example: Pull a red ixora flower from its stalk and taste the tiny sweet drop at the base.
terms.art: A cut-open flower with a small shining drop at the very bottom, and a bee's tongue reaching down to it.

terms.meaning: A fine powder made by flowers. A grain of pollen must reach another flower before seeds can grow.
terms.example: Touch the middle of a hibiscus flower and yellow pollen comes off on your finger.
terms.art: A fingertip with a smear of yellow powder next to the centre of a red hibiscus flower.

terms.meaning: The part of a flower that makes pollen.
terms.example: In a hibiscus, the anthers are the small yellow knobs on the long tube in the middle.
terms.art: A hibiscus flower with an arrow pointing to the small yellow knobs along the central tube.

terms.meaning: The sticky tip in a flower that catches pollen.
terms.example: In a hibiscus, the stigma is the five round red tips at the very end of the tube.
terms.art: The tip of a hibiscus tube seen close, with five round velvety tips and a few yellow grains stuck to them.

terms.meaning: The moving of pollen from an anther to a stigma. After pollination a flower can grow seeds and fruit.
terms.example: A bee carries pollen from one pumpkin flower to another. That is pollination.
terms.art: Two pumpkin flowers with a dotted line from the centre of one to the centre of the other, and a bee flying along the line.

terms.meaning: An animal who carries pollen from flower to flower.
terms.example: Bees, flies, butterflies, moths and some beetles are pollinators. So are some birds and bats.
terms.art: A bee, a fly, a butterfly, a moth and a beetle in a row, each on a different flower.

terms.meaning: The habit of visiting only one kind of flower on one trip.
terms.example: A honeybee working sunflowers flies past the marigolds and goes to the next sunflower.
terms.art: A bee flying over a marigold towards a sunflower, with a dotted path linking three sunflowers.

terms.meaning: Shaking pollen out of a flower by buzzing against it.
terms.example: A big black carpenter bee buzzes on a brinjal flower, and pollen showers out.
terms.art: A large shiny black bee hanging under a purple brinjal flower with a small cloud of yellow dust falling on her.

terms.meaning: An animal who eats dead animals, dropped food or waste.
terms.example: Ants who carry away a dead moth are scavengers.
terms.art: Six ants carrying a dead moth by the wings across a tiled floor.

terms.meaning: A living being who breaks down dead things and waste, so that the material can be used again.
terms.example: Termites are recyclers. They turn a dead branch back into soil.
terms.art: A dead branch on the ground with a crumbling end and pale termites in the soil beneath.

terms.meaning: A name people give to an animal who eats or spoils something people want.
terms.example: A fly is called a pest in a kitchen. The same fly pollinates mango flowers in an orchard.
terms.art: The same green fly drawn twice: once on a plate of food with a cross beside it, and once on mango flowers with a tick beside it.

explanations.concept: What makes an insect an insect
explanations.definition: An insect is an animal with six legs, which are three pairs, and one pair of antennae. Many have wings.
explanations.description: Look closely at an ant on the wall. Count its legs. There are six, in three pairs, and all are joined to the middle part of its body. On its head, it has one pair of antennae. Antennae are two thin feelers that smell and touch the world. Many insects have wings. A fly has one pair, and a grasshopper has two pairs. The front pair of a grasshopper is thin and tough, like a cover for the back pair. Worker ants have no wings. A spider has eight legs and no antennae, so a spider is not an insect. Honeybees, ants, flies and grasshoppers are insects. In this lesson, you will see what some insects do for us, and what they need from us.
examples: An ant with six legs and two thin antennae on a kitchen wall
A housefly with one pair of clear wings
A grasshopper in a field with two pairs of wings, the front pair thin and tough
explanations.art: An ant drawn large, with its six legs numbered in three pairs and its two antennae labelled; beside it a spider with eight legs and a cross.

explanations.concept: A colony is one large family
explanations.definition: A colony is a family of social insects who share one nest. It has one or a few queens who lay eggs, many workers who do the work, and the young.
explanations.description: In a colony of ants or honeybees, the queen is the mother. The workers are her daughters, so they are all sisters. Workers build the nest, clean it, guard it, find food and feed the young. Most workers never lay eggs that grow into new workers. The young begin as eggs and hatch into larvae, who are soft grubs and must be fed. Males are few. A male honeybee is called a drone. Males do no nest work, and they live only to mate with a new queen. A honeybee colony holds tens of thousands of bees. Some ant colonies hold a few dozen ants, and others hold millions. India has several kinds of honeybee. The rock bee builds one huge open comb under a ledge or a water tank. The Indian hive bee nests in hollows and in bee boxes. The tiny stingless bee nests in cracks in walls. Termites also live in colonies, but they are not ants. A termite colony has a king as well as a queen, and termite workers are both female and male.
examples: A line of black ants on a kitchen wall: every ant is a worker, and every worker is a sister.
A rock bee comb under a flyover, covered by a curtain of thousands of bees.
Red weaver ants in a mango tree, living in nests of leaves glued together with silk.
explanations.art: A family portrait of a honeybee colony: one long queen in the middle, many workers around her, two big-eyed drones at the side, and white larvae in cells below.

explanations.concept: How a colony begins, grows and makes new colonies
explanations.definition: A colony begins with one mated queen. It grows as she lays eggs and her daughters raise them. A grown colony makes new queens, and they start new colonies.
explanations.description: After the first heavy rain, winged ants pour out of many nests on the same evening. These are young queens and males, and they mate in the air. Each queen then lands, breaks off her own wings and digs a small hole. She seals herself in and lays her first eggs. She does not eat for weeks. She feeds the first larvae from her own body, using up the muscles that once moved her wings. When her first daughters grow up, they open the nest and bring food. After that the queen only lays eggs. Honeybees start a new colony in another way. The old queen flies off with about half the workers, in a crowd called a swarm. The bees who stay behind raise a new queen. A worker honeybee lives about six weeks in summer. A queen honeybee lives a few years, and an ant queen can live far longer. One black garden ant queen kept in a laboratory lived for 28 years. Workers die every day and new ones hatch, so the colony goes on.
examples: Winged ants and winged termites round a tube light on the first wet evening of the monsoon.
A queen ant alone in a sealed hole with a small heap of eggs.
A swarm of honeybees hanging from a branch like a brown bag while scouts look for a new home.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: winged ants flying after rain, a queen breaking off her wings, the queen in a sealed hole with eggs, and a nest with many workers.

explanations.concept: What workers bring home, and what they build
explanations.definition: Workers collect food for the whole colony, above all for the larvae. They also build a nest that stores the food and protects the young.
explanations.description: A honeybee colony needs two foods from flowers. Nectar is mostly sugar and water, and it gives energy. The bees dry nectar into honey, which keeps for months. Pollen is rich in protein, and it is the food that makes larvae grow. A bee packs pollen into two baskets of stiff hairs on her back legs and carries it home. Honeybees build their comb from wax, which comes out of their own bodies in thin flakes. Each cell has six sides. Some cells hold honey, some hold pollen and some hold one larva each. Ants do not make wax. Most ants dig rooms and tunnels in soil or wood. They carry seeds, dead insects and sweet crumbs home, and they feed the larvae in a nursery room. Weaver ants build in trees. A row of workers pulls two leaves together. Other workers hold larvae in their jaws, and the larvae give out silk that glues the leaves. Many ants also guard small plant-sucking insects and drink the sweet drops they give off.
examples: A honeybee flying home with a yellow lump of pollen on each back leg.
A wax comb with capped honey at the top and larvae in the middle.
A ball of mango leaves in a tree, stitched with white silk, with red ants running over it.
explanations.art: A honeybee seen from the side with a round yellow lump of pollen on her back leg, next to a piece of comb with six-sided cells.

explanations.concept: Pollination: what a flower needs before a fruit can grow
explanations.definition: Pollination is the moving of pollen from an anther to a stigma. After pollination, a flower can grow seeds, and a fruit grows around the seeds.
explanations.description: A flower is the part of a plant that makes seeds. The anthers make pollen, which is a fine powder of tiny grains. The stigma is a sticky tip that catches pollen. When a grain of the right pollen lands on a stigma, it grows a thin tube down into the flower. The tube reaches a tiny egg cell, and a seed begins. A plant cannot walk, so something must carry the pollen. Most plants do better with pollen from another plant of the same kind, and many must have it. A pumpkin vine has two sorts of flower. One sort has only anthers, and the other has only a stigma with a tiny pumpkin below it. Unless pollen travels between them, the tiny pumpkin turns yellow and drops off. Grasses such as rice, wheat and maize let the wind carry their pollen. Nearly nine out of every ten kinds of flowering plant use animals, and most of those animals are insects.
examples: A pumpkin flower with a small green ball under it, waiting for pollen from another pumpkin flower.
Yellow dust on a bee who has just left a sunflower.
A maize plant shaking pollen from the top of the stem into the wind, with no insect needed.
explanations.art: A flower cut in half and labelled: anthers with yellow pollen, a sticky stigma at the top, and a thin tube running down from one pollen grain to an egg cell.

explanations.concept: Why insects make good pollen carriers
explanations.definition: Insects visit flowers to feed. Their hairy bodies pick up pollen at one flower and leave some of it at the next.
explanations.description: A flower offers food. Nectar is a sweet drink, and pollen is a rich meal. A flower also shows where the food is. Bright petals, strong scents and lines on the petals all point to the nectar. Bees see ultraviolet light, which human eyes cannot see, and many flowers carry ultraviolet marks. To reach the nectar, the insect must push past the anthers and the stigma. A bee is covered in hairs, and under a microscope each hair is branched like a tiny feather. Pollen grains catch among the branches. A flying bee also picks up a small electric charge, and pollen can jump a short gap onto her body. She combs most of the pollen into the baskets on her legs. The grains that pollinate are mostly the ones left on parts she cannot reach well. One more habit helps the flower. On one trip, a bee usually keeps to one kind of flower. This is called flower constancy. So pumpkin pollen goes to a pumpkin flower, and not to a marigold.
examples: A bee crawling deep into a pumpkin flower and coming out yellow all over.
Dark lines on a petal that lead towards the middle of the flower.
A honeybee who visits twenty sunflowers in a row and ignores every other flower.
explanations.art: A greatly enlarged bee hair that branches like a feather, with round spiky pollen grains caught among the branches.

explanations.concept: Many pollinators, each suited to some flowers
explanations.definition: A pollinator is any animal who carries pollen between flowers. Honeybees are only one kind among many thousands.
explanations.description: There are about 20,000 kinds of bee in the world, and most of them do not live in colonies. Each mother builds a small nest alone. Some flowers hold their pollen inside closed tubes with a small hole at the tip. Brinjal and tomato flowers are like this. A honeybee cannot get that pollen out. A carpenter bee can. She grips the flower and buzzes her flight muscles a few hundred times each second, and the pollen showers out. This is buzz pollination. Flies are pollinators too. Mango flowers are small and open, with nectar that a short mouth can reach. In many orchards most of the visitors are flies. Cocoa flowers are pollinated by midges, which are tiny flies, so chocolate depends on them. Hawkmoths pollinate pale, scented flowers that open at night. Butterflies, beetles and wasps carry pollen as well. Every kind of fig tree is pollinated by one special kind of tiny fig wasp. Some birds and bats are pollinators, though they are not insects.
examples: A large shiny black carpenter bee buzzing loudly on a brinjal flower.
Green flies and striped hoverflies on a bunch of mango flowers.
A hawkmoth hovering at a jasmine flower after dark with her long tongue unrolled.
explanations.art: Four flowers with four visitors: a carpenter bee on a brinjal flower, a green fly on mango flowers, a hawkmoth at a jasmine flower and a butterfly on a red ixora.

explanations.concept: How much of our food needs insect pollinators
explanations.definition: About three out of every four main kinds of food crop give more or better food when animals pollinate them. Most of those animals are insects.
explanations.description: In 2007 a team of scientists checked the world's main food crops. Of 115 crops, 87 gained from animal pollinators. That is about three out of every four. Mango, pumpkin, cucumber, apple, mustard, coriander, cardamom, coffee and almonds are all on that list. Some of these crops give almost nothing without pollinators. Others give a smaller or poorer harvest. The same study found something that surprises many people. By weight, only about one third of the world's food comes from those crops. The reason is that people eat huge amounts of rice, wheat and maize, and these are pollinated by the wind. Bananas grow their fruit with no pollination at all, and potatoes grow from pieces of potato. So people would not starve without pollinators. But most fruits, many vegetables, nuts, oil seeds and spices would become rare and costly. Those foods hold many of the vitamins that our bodies need.
examples: Cardamom from the hills of Kerala, which sets very few pods without bees.
Apple growers in Himachal Pradesh, who rent bee boxes when their trees flower.
A plate of plain rice, which needed wind and no insect.
explanations.art: A dinner plate split in two: on one side rice, roti and a banana, and on the other side mango, pumpkin curry, mustard seeds, cardamom pods and a cup of coffee, with a small bee above that side.

explanations.definition: A recycler breaks down dead things and waste, so that the material can be used again. Many insects are recyclers.
explanations.description: Every day, leaves fall, animals leave dung, and animals die. Insects are often the first to arrive. Ants are scavengers, which means they eat dead animals and dropped food. Workers cut up a dead moth, carry the pieces home and feed them to the larvae. Flies lay eggs on dead animals and rotting food. The eggs hatch into larvae called maggots, and the maggots eat the soft parts within days. Dung beetles bury dung in the ground, where it feeds the soil. Termites eat dead wood and dry leaves, with the help of microbes and fungi. Most kinds of cockroach live in forests and eat rotting leaves. These insects cut dead things into small pieces, bury them and spread them. Fungi and bacteria then finish the work, and plants take up what is left. Insects do a great deal of this work in cities too. Scientists in New York studied ants and other small animals on a few streets. In a year these animals ate dropped food equal to 60,000 hot dogs.
examples: Ants taking a dead cockroach apart on a kitchen floor.
A fallen coconut frond with termites and soil under it.
A dung beetle rolling a ball of cow dung along a path.
explanations.art: A strip of ground seen from the side: ants carrying a dead beetle, a dung beetle with a dung ball, termites under a dead branch and maggots on a fallen fruit.

explanations.concept: One insect can do two jobs
explanations.definition: Many insects have a young stage and an adult stage that eat different foods. So the same insect can be a recycler when young and a pollinator when grown.
explanations.description: A green blowfly lays her eggs on a dead fish or a dead rat. Her maggots eat it and grow fast. In warm weather they turn into flies in about two weeks. The adult fly feeds in a different way. She drinks sweet liquids, and flower nectar is one of them. Her body is covered in bristles, and pollen sticks to them. In a mango orchard she is one of the main pollinators. Hoverflies are striped like bees. The larvae of many hoverflies live in dirty water and rotting plants and feed there. The adults hover at flowers and carry pollen. The same is true of many beetles. A heap of rotting kitchen waste and a tree full of flowers can both belong to one insect's life. People call the fly a pest in the kitchen, because she can carry germs to food. In the orchard she is doing work that the tree needs.
examples: A shiny green fly with yellow pollen on her bristles, walking over mango flowers.
White maggots clearing a dead fish on a rubbish heap in two or three days.
A striped hoverfly hanging in the air in front of a coriander flower.
explanations.art: A circle of four pictures joined by arrows: fly eggs on a fish head, white maggots, a brown pupa in soil, and a green adult fly on mango flowers.

explanations.concept: What harms insect workers, and what helps them
explanations.definition: Insects are harmed by poison sprays, by the loss of flowers and nesting places, and by bright lights at night. They are helped by flowers, by unsprayed places and by darkness.
explanations.description: A pesticide is a poison used to kill insects who eat crops. Most pesticides also kill bees, flies and ants, and the insects who hunt the crop-eaters. Some pesticides do not kill a bee at once. They harm her memory, so that she cannot find her way home. A colony needs flowers in every month of the year. When a field grows only one crop, there are flowers for two weeks and then none. Street lights pull moths away from the flowers they would pollinate at night. In 63 nature reserves in Germany, scientists weighed the flying insects they caught each year. After 27 years the weight had fallen by about three quarters. There are few such counts from India, so nobody knows the full picture here. Some farmers use insects in place of poison. Fruit growers in China have put weaver ant nests in their orange trees for about 1,700 years. The ants hunt the insects who eat the fruit. A family can help by growing flowering plants, and by never spraying a plant that is in flower. Trees help too, because they are homes. A mango tree gives shade and shelter. Weaver ants stitch their nests in its leaves, and a crow or a myna can build a nest in its branches. A squirrel runs along them. Cutting down a tree takes away all these homes at once.
examples: A tulsi or curry leaf plant left to flower on a balcony, with small bees on it.
A farmer who sprays in the evening, after the bees have gone home, and never on open flowers.
A weaver ant nest left in a mango tree, because the ants hunt fruit-eating insects.
explanations.art: A balcony with flowering tulsi, curry leaf and marigold pots, with small bees and a butterfly visiting them.

explanations.concept: Pests: when insects and animals eat the crop
explanations.context: This card comes after what harms insects. Farmers do have real trouble from pests, and some ways of fighting pests do not harm bees.
explanations.definition: A pest eats or spoils a crop. A farmer can guard a crop in ways that do not poison the pollinators.
explanations.description: Insects such as caterpillars and aphids eat leaves and suck sap. Bigger animals also eat crops. In north India, the neel gai, a large blue-grey antelope, walks into wheat and mustard fields at night. Monkeys raid fruit and maize. A farmer who loses her crop loses her year's food and money, so she must keep watch. Some ways are safe for bees. She can pick caterpillars off by hand. She can spray neem, a mix made from crushed neem seeds, on leaves in the evening, when the bees have gone home. She can hang yellow sticky cards to catch small flying insects. She can leave weaver ants in the trees, because they hunt fruit-eating insects. For neel gai and monkeys, a fence, a net or a night watch works better than any spray, since they are not insects. Spraying neem on open flowers can still harm bees, so spray only the leaves.
examples: A farmer picking caterpillars off cabbage leaves by hand, then spraying neem on the leaves in the evening
A family taking turns to watch a wheat field at night, because neel gai come in the dark
A yellow sticky card hung among brinjal plants to catch whiteflies
explanations.art: A farmer at dusk spraying neem on cabbage leaves, a neel gai at the edge of a wheat field with a fence, and a yellow sticky card hanging among plants.

explanations.concept: Are honeybees enough, or do crops need wild pollinators too?
explanations.definition: Farmers and scientists agree that crops need pollinators. They disagree about how far kept honeybees can replace wild insects.
explanations.description: Honeybees can be kept in boxes and moved to a field on the day the flowers open. That makes them very useful to farmers. But a study of 600 fields in many countries, published in 2013, gave a surprise. Fruit grew better in every crop that wild insects visited more often. Honeybee visits made a clear difference in only about one crop in seven.
examples: An apple grower who rents bee boxes for two weeks each spring.
A brinjal field beside a patch of wild shrubs, where carpenter bees nest in dead wood.

perspectives.explanation: Kept honeybees are the pollinators we can count on. A farmer can bring 40,000 bees to a field in one box, on the right day. Wild insects come and go, and nobody can order them.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study wild pollinators, such as Lucas Garibaldi and his team
perspectives.explanation: Wild bees and flies often pollinate better at each visit. They work in cool or windy weather, and some can buzz pollen out of flowers that honeybees cannot open. Bee boxes add to their work and do not replace it.
Very many kept honeybees in one place may take the nectar and pollen that wild bees need. So bringing more hives can sometimes harm the wild pollinators nearby. This is still being tested.

explanations.art: A field of yellow mustard with a row of white bee boxes on one side and a strip of wild flowering shrubs with different bees and flies on the other.

explanations.definition: A superorganism is a group of animals that lives so closely together that the group behaves like one body. Scientists disagree about whether a colony should be called one.
explanations.description: A worker bee cannot live long alone, and she usually has no young of her own. The colony as a whole feeds, grows, keeps itself warm and makes new colonies. In 1911 the American ant scientist William Morton Wheeler wrote that an ant colony is like one living body.
examples: A honeybee colony keeps the nursery at about 35 degrees Celsius, summer and winter, as a body keeps its warmth.
A colony that splits into two swarms, as one cell splits into two cells.

perspectives.who: William Morton Wheeler in 1911, and later Bert Hölldobler and Edward O. Wilson
perspectives.explanation: The colony is the animal. The queen is like the part of a body that makes young. The workers are like the parts that feed and defend the body. What grows, survives and has young is the colony.

Each bee and each ant is a whole animal. She senses, learns, remembers and chooses for herself. Workers in one nest sometimes even struggle against each other. Calling the colony one body hides all of this.
Both ways of looking are useful. Your own body is a colony of billions of cells, and each cell is alive. Whether we see one being or many depends on how closely we look.

explanations.art: A honeybee swarm hanging from a branch, drawn so that the whole swarm has the faint outline of one large animal.

agreed.text: Most flowers cannot make seeds unless pollen is carried to the stigma. Insects carry the pollen for most kinds of flowering plant.
agreed.evidence: Scientists cover flowers with fine net bags, so that insects cannot reach them. Many kinds of plant then set few seeds or none. A count published in 2011 found that nearly nine in ten kinds of flowering plant are pollinated by animals.

agreed.text: About three out of four of the world's main food crops give more or better food with animal pollinators.
agreed.evidence: In 2007 Alexandra-Maria Klein and her team checked 115 leading crops. They found that 87 of them gain from animal pollination.

agreed.text: In a honeybee or ant colony the workers are daughters of the queen.
agreed.evidence: Beekeepers and scientists have watched queens laying eggs in hives with glass walls. Tests of the workers' genes show that they share one mother.

agreed.text: A colony lives much longer than its workers do.
agreed.evidence: Scientists mark young bees with dots of paint. In summer the marked bees are gone in about six weeks, and the colony is still there.

agreed.text: A hairy body carries more pollen than a smooth one, and bee hairs are branched.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, bee hairs look like tiny feathers with pollen grains caught in them. Counts of pollen on insects' bodies show that hairier insects carry more.

agreed.text: Insects remove a large share of the dead animals, dung and dropped food around us.
agreed.evidence: Scientists put out weighed food in cages that let insects in and keep bigger animals out. The food still disappears, and they weigh how much has gone.

challenging.claim: If bees disappeared, humans would die out within four years.
challenging.who: A saying often printed with Albert Einstein's name.
challenging.for: About three out of four main crops gain from animal pollinators. Without them, fruits, nuts and many vegetables would become scarce.
challenging.against: No record shows that Einstein said or wrote this. Rice, wheat and maize are pollinated by wind and give most of the world's food by weight. People would eat a much poorer diet, but they would not die out.

challenging.claim: Honeybees do nearly all the pollinating that matters.
challenging.who: A common belief, and the view of some farm advisers.
challenging.for: Honeybees are many, they visit a great range of flowers, and farmers can move them to a field in boxes.
challenging.against: A 2013 study of 600 fields found that wild insects raised the fruit harvest in every crop studied. Honeybee visits did so in about one crop in seven.

challenging.claim: Flies are dirty pests with no use.
challenging.who: A common belief in homes and shops.
challenging.for: Houseflies walk on waste and then on food, and they can carry germs that make people ill.
challenging.against: Fly maggots clear away dead animals and rotting food. Adult flies are main pollinators of mango, cocoa and many other plants. Keeping flies off food is wise. Wiping out flies would cost us fruit.

challenging.who: The everyday name for termites in English and in several Indian languages.
challenging.for: Termites are small, live in big colonies with a queen, and build nests in soil, as ants do.
challenging.against: Termites are close relatives of cockroaches. Ants are close relatives of wasps and bees. A termite colony has a king, and termite workers are both female and male.

challenging.claim: An ant colony is really one animal.
challenging.who: William Morton Wheeler in 1911, and Bert Hölldobler and Edward O. Wilson in their 2008 book The Superorganism.
challenging.for: The colony feeds, grows, defends itself and makes new colonies. A single worker cannot do these things alone.
challenging.against: Each ant senses, learns and chooses. Workers sometimes lay their own eggs, and other workers remove them. So the members do not always act as one.

challenging.claim: Spraying poison is the best way to protect a crop from insects.
challenging.who: Many sellers of pesticides, and many farmers since the 1950s.
challenging.for: A spray works within hours, and it can save a crop that is being eaten.
challenging.against: Sprays also kill pollinators and the insects who hunt the crop-eaters. The crop-eaters often return in greater numbers. Farmers who keep weaver ants, or who spray less, can harvest as much fruit.

big_questions.q: A bee goes to a flower for food, and the flower gets pollinated. Who is helping whom?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one gains, and whether either of them needs to know about the other's gain.

big_questions.q: A worker bee lives about six weeks, and her colony lives for years. Which one is the animal?
big_questions.hint: Your skin cells live a few weeks, and you live for many years.

big_questions.q: A fly's young eat a rotting fish, and the grown fly pollinates mango flowers. Is she a pest or a helper?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is giving the name. A cook in a kitchen and a farmer in an orchard see the same fly very differently.

big_questions.q: People call an insect a pest when she eats our crop. What might she call us?
big_questions.hint: A field of one crop is a huge meal to an insect. A spray is a danger to her whole family.

big_questions.q: Wild bees pollinate a whole village's crops for no pay. If one farmer's spray kills them, who has lost something?
big_questions.hint: Think about things that everybody uses and nobody owns, such as clean air.

big_questions.q: If every recycler stopped work for one year, what would your street look like?
big_questions.hint: Count the leaves, the dung, the dropped food and the dead insects of one day, and multiply.

story.title: The Flies in the Mango Flowers
story.note: Yazhini, Karthik, Paati and their orchard are made up, and so is the habit of Paati's mother. These facts are real: mango trees around Krishnagiri in Tamil Nadu flower in the cool months and fruit in summer. Mango flowers are tiny and open, and each bunch holds hundreds or thousands of them. In many orchards most of the visitors are flies, including green blowflies and striped hoverflies, with some small bees. Blowfly maggots feed on dead fish and other dead animals. Mango growers in some countries put out rotting fish or meat at flowering time to bring more flies.
text: Every February, Paati's forty mango trees near Krishnagiri changed colour. The dark green turned pale gold, because every branch ended in a bunch of flowers. Each bunch was as long as Yazhini's arm, and each one held more tiny flowers than she could count.
This February her cousin Karthik had come from Chennai for a week. He was eleven, two years older than Yazhini, and he did not like the orchard at all.
"It smells," he said on the first morning.

He was right. Behind the cowshed, Paati kept a heap. Fish heads went on the heap, and fruit skins, and old straw from the cow's stall. Shiny green flies sat on it in the sun. The day before, Yazhini had turned the heap with a stick. Fat white maggots were wriggling in the fish heads, and she had covered them again quickly.
"Flies carry germs," Karthik said. "At home we would spray them. Paati, shall I ask Mama to bring a can from town?"
Paati was tying up the calf. "We will see," she said.
Yazhini wanted her cousin to like the orchard. "Tomorrow I will help you bury the heap," she told him. "Today I have school work."

Her teacher, Revathi Miss, had asked every child to choose one tree in flower. They had to watch one bunch of flowers for fifteen minutes and put a stroke in the notebook for every visitor. Yazhini had already ruled three columns. Bees. Butterflies. Others.
She chose the old Neelum tree by the well, because one bunch hung low enough to see. Karthik came too. He held his nose as a joke, though the heap was far behind them.
For a minute, nobody came. Then someone landed, and Yazhini lifted her pencil over 'Bees'.
The visitor was not a bee. She was a green fly, as shiny as a new steel plate. She walked over the tiny flowers and dipped her mouth into one after another.
"Shoo," said Karthik, and raised his hand.
"Don't! I have to count her." Yazhini put a stroke under 'Others'.

Another green fly came. Then a smaller fly, striped like a bee, who hung in the air before she landed. Then two more green ones. A small dark bee arrived, worked quickly along the bunch and left. Ants walked up and down the stalk.
After fifteen minutes Yazhini added up her strokes. Bees, 4. Butterflies, 0. Others, 23. She counted the 'Others' again from memory. Four were ants. Nineteen were flies.
"Your tree is dirty," said Karthik.
Yazhini did not answer. One green fly had stopped on a flower just in front of her nose. The fly's back was covered in short stiff hairs. Stuck all over the hairs was a fine yellow dust.
The fly stepped across to the next flower. A little of the yellow dust stayed behind, on the tip in the middle of the flower she had left.
Yazhini looked back towards the cowshed. She looked at the flies in the tree. She looked at the cowshed again.
"Karthik," she said slowly. "What do bees do for flowers?"
"They carry pollen. Everyone knows that. Then the fruit comes."
"Look at her back."
He bent close and looked for a long moment. "That is pollen," he said. "On a fly."

"These flowers are small and flat, like tiny plates," said Yazhini. "A fly has a short mouth, and she can still reach the sweet drop. A bee is not the only one who can carry pollen." She pointed with her pencil. "And where do green flies come from?"
Karthik thought of the fish heads. "Maggots," he said, and made a face.
"The maggots in our heap. They eat the fish heads until only bones are left. Then they turn into these." She tapped the notebook. "Nineteen of them. On one bunch."
They ran to Paati with the notebook. Paati read the three columns twice. Then she laughed until she had to sit down on the step.
"My mother never let anyone clear that heap before the mangoes had set," she said. "She said the trees liked it. I thought it was only her habit."
"So no can from town?" asked Karthik.
"Nobody sprays a tree in flower," said Paati. "Not in this orchard."
Karthik looked towards the cowshed for a while. "It still smells," he said.
"Yes," said Yazhini. "Like mangoes in May."
That night she opened her notebook again. She crossed out 'Others' and wrote 'Flies' and 'Ants'. Then she ruled a fourth column for tomorrow, and above it she wrote: Where did each visitor grow up?
story.epiphany: The flies that Karthik wanted to spray were pollinating the mango flowers. Their young, the maggots, were clearing the fish heads in the heap. One insect did both jobs: she was a recycler when young and a pollinator when grown.
ask: Why can a fly reach the nectar of a mango flower, though her mouth is short?
What would happen to the mango harvest if every fly in the orchard were sprayed in February?
Which other animal near your home do people call a pest? What work might that animal do?
