games.title: Whose Work Is This? The insect job cards
games.context: This is a card game about the work insects do. Each card describes an insect doing something, and you say whether it is colony work, pollinating or recycling.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with three small tokens marked Colony work, Pollinating and Recycling in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 20 job cards: what an insect is doing on the front, the kind of work and the reason on the back

items.f: A honeybee worker fans her wings over a cell of thin nectar.
items.b: Colony work. The moving air dries the nectar into honey for the colony's store.

items.f: A big black carpenter bee grips a brinjal flower and buzzes loudly.
items.b: Pollinating. Her buzz shakes pollen out of the flower's closed tubes.

items.f: A line of ants drags a dead cockroach across a kitchen floor.
items.b: Recycling. The ants cut up the body and feed it to their larvae.

items.f: A dung beetle rolls a ball of cow dung away and buries the ball.
items.b: Recycling. Buried dung feeds the soil and the beetle's young.

items.f: A green blowfly walks over a bunch of mango flowers, sipping from each.
items.b: Pollinating. Pollen sticks to her bristles and reaches the next flower.

items.f: Weaver ants pull two mango leaves together. Other ants glue the edges with silk.
items.b: Colony work. They are building a leaf nest for the colony.

items.f: Termite workers chew the underside of a dead branch on the ground.
items.b: Recycling. Termites, with the microbes they carry, turn dead wood into soil.

items.f: After the first rain, a queen ant breaks off her own wings and digs a small hole.
items.b: Colony work. She is starting a new colony by herself.

items.f: A hawkmoth hovers at a jasmine flower after dark, with her long tongue unrolled.
items.b: Pollinating. Pale, scented night flowers are pollinated by moths.

items.f: Maggots eat a dead fish on a rubbish heap until only bones are left.
items.b: Recycling. The young of flies clear dead animals in a few days.

items.f: A young worker bee puts her head into a wax cell and feeds the larva inside.
items.b: Colony work. Nurse bees feed every larva many times a day.

items.f: A midge smaller than a sesame seed crawls into a cocoa flower.
items.b: Pollinating. Cocoa trees depend on midges, so chocolate does too.

items.f: Honeybees at the hive entrance touch each arriving bee with their antennae.
items.b: Colony work. Guards let in only bees who smell of their own colony.

items.f: A stingless bee flies home with a yellow lump of pollen on each back leg.
items.b: Colony work and pollinating. The lumps feed the larvae, and loose grains on her body reached other flowers. Either token scores.

items.f: A cockroach on a forest floor eats a soft, rotting leaf.
items.b: Recycling. Most kinds of cockroach live outdoors and eat dead leaves.

items.f: A plain tiger butterfly drinks from a red ixora flower.
items.b: Pollinating. Pollen sticks to her legs and her long tongue.

items.f: Thousands of rock bees hang in a thick curtain over their open comb.
items.b: Colony work. Their bodies are the wall that keeps the comb warm and safe.

items.f: A honeybee visits only pumpkin flowers all morning and flies past every other flower.
items.b: Pollinating. Keeping to one kind of flower takes pumpkin pollen to pumpkin flowers.

items.f: Fat brown larvae of the black soldier fly eat vegetable peels in a compost bin.
items.b: Recycling. These larvae turn kitchen waste into compost quickly.

items.f: Worker ants carry dead nestmates and rubbish to a heap far from the nursery.
items.b: Colony work. A clean nest keeps the larvae from falling ill.

printables.title: 3 work tokens: Colony work, Pollinating, Recycling. Print one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one work token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the kind of work on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also gives the reason scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the kind of work aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right answer.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 20 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens.
flow.say: Each card shows an insect at work. Your three tokens are three kinds of work: colony work, pollinating and recycling. We will say which kind each card shows.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whose Work Is This. You set up the job cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a work token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide which kind of work the insect was doing?
good: I asked who gains from it: the nest, a flower or the soil.
If she is on a flower, pollen may be moving.
If she is eating something dead, she is recycling.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: who gains from this? If the colony gains, it is colony work. If a flower gains, it is pollinating. If something dead is being cleared, it is recycling. One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Whose Work Is This you play the first ten job cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. This time, also give the reason. Say what the work is for. A good reason earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Say what each job is for.
flow.context: In this step of Whose Work Is This you play the last ten cards and give a reason for each.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 20 cards into three piles by kind of work and look at the piles.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into three piles. Look at the pollinating pile. Which of them are honeybees? Who are the others?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three piles. Count the honeybees in the pollinating pile.

check.q: Which of these insects recycles when young and pollinates when grown?
check.why: A blowfly's maggots eat dead animals, and the adult fly drinks nectar and carries pollen. A queen ant lays eggs. A termite worker eats dead wood all through their life.

flow.context: This is the last step of Whose Work Is This. You sort the job cards by kind of work and compare the piles.

games.title: Flower Loyal: a bee's memory game
games.context: This is a memory game about flower constancy. A bee who keeps to one kind of flower pollinates more flowers, and in this game so do you.

setup.art: Twenty-four small cards lying face down on a table in four rows of six.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the 24 flower cards. Lay them face down in four rows of six.

setup.art: A child turning over one card that reads Pumpkin flower, with her other hand reaching for a second card.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over one card. That is your flower for this trip. Now turn over another.

setup.art: Three face-up cards that all read Pumpkin flower in one child's hand, and one face-up card reading Mango flower still on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Keep turning cards while they match. A card of another kind ends your trip.

printables.title: 24 flower cards: 6 pumpkin flowers, 6 mango flowers, 6 sunflowers and 6 brinjal flowers
Score sheet: flowers pollinated on each trip
items: Player ___. Trip 1: ___ flowers. Trip 2: ___ flowers. Trip 3: ___ flowers.
Player ___. Trip 1: ___ flowers. Trip 2: ___ flowers. Trip 3: ___ flowers.
Playing alone: number of trips to clear the table: ___

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and lay them face down in four rows of six. Each player is a bee.
On your turn you make one trip. Turn over one card. The kind of flower on that card is your flower for this trip.
Turn over another card. If it is the same kind, you have carried pollen to it. Leave it face up and turn over another.
Your trip ends when you turn over a different kind of flower. Pollen from a pumpkin cannot pollinate a mango.
At the end of your trip, pick up the matching cards if you have two or more. Score 1 point for each card after the first. Turn any other face-up cards face down again, in their places.
If your very first two cards differ, you score nothing. Turn both face down again.
Play until fewer than two cards of every kind are left. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Count how many trips you need to clear the table. Then play again and try to use fewer trips.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 flower cards. Shuffle them and lay them face down in four rows of six.
flow.say: You are a bee. On each trip you choose one kind of flower. Pollen from a pumpkin flower can only pollinate another pumpkin flower. So you score when you find the same kind again.
flow.kid: Lay 24 cards face down. You are a bee looking for flowers.
flow.context: This is the first step of Flower Loyal. You lay out the flower cards.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules. Remind players to return unmatched cards to the same places.
flow.say: Turn over your first card. Which flower is yours for this trip? Now try to find another of the same kind. Remember where the others are lying.
flow.kid: Turn a card. Find more of the same kind. Remember where each flower is.

ask.q: What helps you to make a long trip with many matches?
good: Remembering where each kind of flower is.
Choosing a first card whose partners I have already seen.
Keeping to one kind and not turning cards at random.

flow.parent: Early trips are short, because nobody knows where the flowers are. Trips get longer as players remember. A real bee also learns where her flowers grow and returns to them.
flow.context: In this step of Flower Loyal you make trips and try to find flowers of one kind.

flow.do: Count the points. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: On your best trip, how many flowers did you pollinate? What would a real flower gain from a bee who keeps to one kind?
flow.kid: Count your points.

check.q: A bee carries pumpkin pollen to a marigold. What happens to that pollen?
check.why: Pollen works only on a flower of the same kind. Pumpkin pollen on a marigold makes no seed, so it is wasted. This is why flower constancy matters so much to a plant.

flow.context: This is the last step of Flower Loyal. You count your points and say why keeping to one kind of flower matters.

experiments.title: Hairy or Smooth: which carrier takes pollen to more flowers?
experiments.question: Haldi powder is the pollen, and a row of 15 paper boxes is a row of flowers. One carrier is a fuzzy cotton bud and the other is the smooth end of a plastic pen. After one dip in the haldi, how many boxes does each carrier mark?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many boxes out of 15 will the cotton bud mark with yellow? How many will the smooth pen mark? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same haldi and the same paper for both carriers. Dip each carrier once, press it into the haldi and turn it once. Knock it once on the rim of the katori, so that loose powder falls off. Press and turn once in each box, with the same gentle push. Never dip again in the middle of a row. Do three rows with each carrier, because one row can be a fluke. Use a fresh cotton head for each row, and wipe the pen dry before each row. Only the carrier changes.

materials.item: haldi (turmeric) powder, 1 level teaspoon, in a small katori. Kumkum also works
cotton buds. Each bud has two cotton heads, and you need three heads
a plastic pen with a smooth, rounded back end. The end of a steel spoon handle also works
a sheet of white paper, a ruler and a pencil
an old newspaper to work on, and a dry cloth to wipe the pen

experiments.safety: Haldi stains cloth and some table tops. Work on newspaper and wear old clothes.
experiments.record: Draw a table with two rows, one for the cotton bud and one for the pen. Write the number of boxes marked in each of the three tries. Then write the middle value of the three.
experiments.context: In this experiment haldi powder stands for pollen. You test which carries the haldi to more paper boxes in a row: a fuzzy cotton bud or a smooth pen end. You will find out why bees are hairy.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper with six ruled rows of fifteen small square boxes, three rows labelled Bud and three labelled Pen, beside a ruler and a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Rule 6 rows of 15 boxes. Make each box 1 centimetre wide.

setup.art: A child pressing the cotton head of a cotton bud into a small steel katori of yellow haldi powder.
setup.caption: 2. Press the cotton bud into the haldi and turn it once. Knock it once on the rim.

setup.art: The child pressing the yellow cotton bud into the third box of a row, with yellow marks already in the first two boxes.
setup.caption: 3. Press and turn once in box 1, then box 2, and so on to box 15. Do not dip again.

setup.art: The child pressing the rounded back end of a plastic pen into the first box of another row, leaving a faint yellow mark.
setup.caption: 4. Do the same with the smooth end of the pen.

setup.art: The finished sheet held at arm's length: long rows of yellow marks beside Bud and short rows beside Pen, with a count written at the end of each row.
setup.caption: 5. Hold the paper at arm's length. Count the boxes where you can see yellow.

flow.do: Show your child the haldi, a cotton bud and the pen. Explain the test. Ask for the two guesses and the reason, and write them down.
flow.say: The haldi is our pollen. Each box will be one flower. We dip a carrier once and then visit 15 flowers in a row. How many boxes will the cotton bud mark? How many will the pen mark? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Haldi is the pollen. Guess how many boxes each carrier will mark. Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that carrier will mark more boxes?
good: The cotton is fluffy, so more powder will stick.
The pen is smooth, so the powder will slide off.
The cotton has gaps where the powder can hide.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Many children expect both carriers to run out after two or three boxes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hairy or Smooth test. You guess how many paper boxes each carrier will mark with haldi, before you test.

flow.do: Spread the newspaper. On the white paper, rule 6 rows of 15 boxes, each box 1 centimetre wide. Write Bud beside three rows and Pen beside three rows. Put 1 level teaspoon of haldi in the katori.
flow.say: We need six rows of flowers. Three rows are for the cotton bud and three are for the pen.
flow.kid: Rule 6 rows of 15 boxes. Label three rows Bud and three rows Pen.

ask.q: Why three rows for each carrier?
good: One try can be a fluke.
If three tries agree, we can trust the result more.

flow.parent: A page from a maths notebook with squares saves the ruling. The boxes only need to be about the width of a fingertip.
flow.context: In this step of the Hairy or Smooth test you rule the rows of paper boxes that stand for flowers.

flow.do: Press one cotton head into the haldi and turn it once. Knock the stick once on the rim. Press and turn the head once in box 1, then in box 2, and on to box 15. Do the second and third Bud rows with fresh cotton heads.
flow.say: Dip once, turn once and knock once. Now visit every flower in the row. Press, turn and move on. Use the same gentle push each time, and do not dip again.
flow.kid: Dip the cotton bud once. Press and turn in each box. Do not dip again.
flow.parent: Let your child do all the pressing, so that the push is the same for both carriers. The marks get fainter along the row. That is expected.
flow.context: In this step of the Hairy or Smooth test you carry haldi along three rows of boxes. You use a cotton bud.

flow.do: Wipe the back end of the pen with the dry cloth. Press it into the haldi, turn it once and knock it once on the rim. Press and turn once in each box of a Pen row. Wipe the pen and repeat for the other two Pen rows.
flow.say: Now the smooth carrier. Do everything exactly as before. Dip once, turn once and knock once. Then press and turn in every box.
flow.kid: Wipe the pen. Dip it once. Press and turn in each box.

check.q: In the Hairy or Smooth test, why do you knock each carrier once on the rim?
options: So loose powder falls off both
So the katori makes a sound
check.why: A flying insect loses loose pollen on the way. The knock removes loose powder from both carriers in the same way, so the test is fair. If you chose 'sticks harder', remember that a knock shakes powder off.

flow.parent: The pen end must be dry. A damp or oily pen picks up a thick coat of haldi, and the test then compares wet with dry.
flow.context: In this step of the Hairy or Smooth test you carry haldi along three rows of boxes. You use the smooth end of a pen.

flow.do: Hold the paper at arm's length. In each row, count the boxes where your child can see yellow. Write the six numbers in the table. For each carrier, circle the middle value of the three.
flow.say: Hold the paper out at arm's length. A box counts if you can see yellow from there. Count each row and write the number. Which of the three numbers is in the middle?
flow.kid: Hold the paper far out. Count the yellow boxes in each row.
flow.parent: The middle value is the one left when you cross out the biggest and the smallest. In most homes the cotton bud marks 8 to 15 boxes and the pen marks 1 to 4. Write what you really get.
flow.context: In this step of the Hairy or Smooth test you count how many boxes each carrier marked with haldi.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Then say why you think it happened. Which carrier is more like a bee? What does a bee have that the pen does not?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Where on the cotton bud did the haldi stay?
good: Between the threads of the cotton.
Deep inside the fluff, and it came out a little at a time.

ask.q: A bee is hairy and a beetle's back is smooth and shiny. Which is likely to carry more pollen?
good: The bee, because pollen catches in her hairs.

flow.parent: The reason: cotton is made of thousands of fine threads, and powder is held in the gaps between them. Each press lets a little out, so the marks go on for many boxes. The smooth pen holds powder only on its skin, and the first one or two presses take it all. A bee is covered in hairs, and each hair is branched like a tiny feather. Pollen catches among the hairs and comes off a little at a time, flower after flower. Keep the sheet. It is used again in the worksheets.
flow.think: The cotton bud did not put all its haldi in box 1. Why is that good for flowers 2 to 15?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hairy or Smooth test. You say what your counts show about hairy and smooth carriers.

experiments.title: The Clean-up Count: how fast do ants clear 20 crumbs?
experiments.question: Twenty small crumbs are left on a paper near an ant line. How many minutes pass before all 20 are gone? Do the crumbs go at a steady speed, or does the work start slowly and then speed up?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many minutes will the ants take to clear all 20 crumbs? Will the crumbs go at the same speed all the time, or faster later? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use 20 crumbs of the same food and the same size on each of two paper squares. Put paper A on the floor, about 30 centimetres from the ant line. Put paper B on an upturned katori standing in a plate of water, so that ants cannot reach it. Paper B shows whether crumbs vanish with no ants. Count every 5 minutes by the clock. Do not touch the papers, blow on the ants or stand in their path.

materials.item: squares of white paper, each about 10 centimetres wide
crumbs of a plain biscuit, or shreds of fresh grated coconut, each no bigger than a sesame seed
a steel katori and a steel plate with a rim, with water 1 centimetre deep in the plate
a place where ants walk: a kitchen corner, a window sill, a balcony or a doorstep
a clock or phone timer, a pencil and a notebook page
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.record: Draw a table with nine rows, for 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 and 40 minutes. At each time, write the number of ants on paper A and the number of crumbs left on each paper. Then draw a line graph of the crumbs left on paper A.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put 20 crumbs near an ant line and count every 5 minutes. You find out how fast the ants clear the crumbs away, and whether they hurry or go steadily.

setup.art: A paper square on a kitchen floor with twenty tiny crumbs spread over it, about a ruler's length away from a line of small ants along the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Put 20 crumbs on paper A. Lay it 30 centimetres from the ant line.

setup.art: A second paper square with twenty crumbs resting on an upturned steel katori that stands in a steel plate of water.
setup.caption: 2. Put paper B, with 20 crumbs, on a katori standing in water. Ants cannot cross the water.

setup.art: A child kneeling a little way back from paper A with a notebook, counting ants on the paper while a phone timer shows 10 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Every 5 minutes, count the ants on paper A and the crumbs left.

setup.art: A notebook page with a line graph that stays flat at 20, then drops steeply to 0, with minutes along the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Draw a line graph of the crumbs left on paper A.

flow.do: Find a place where ants are walking. Show your child the crumbs. Ask for the guesses and the reason, and write them down.
flow.say: We will leave 20 crumbs near these ants. How many minutes will they take to clear all 20? Will the crumbs go at a steady speed, or faster later? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how long the ants need for 20 crumbs. Steady, or faster later? Why?

ask.q: What has to happen before the first crumb goes?
good: An ant has to find the paper.
She has to tell the others, or lead them there.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If you see no ants indoors, try a balcony, a doorstep or the foot of a tree near your gate. Evening is often a busy time for ants.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Clean-up Count. You guess how fast ants will clear 20 crumbs, before you test.

flow.do: Count 20 crumbs onto each paper and spread them out. Lay paper A on the floor, 30 centimetres from the ant line. Stand the katori upside down in the plate of water, and lay paper B on top. Start the timer.
flow.say: Paper A is for the ants. Paper B stands in water, so no ant can get to that paper.
flow.kid: Put 20 crumbs on each paper. Paper A goes near the ants. Paper B stands in water.

ask.q: What will paper B tell us?
good: Whether crumbs disappear when no ants come.
If B keeps all 20, then the ants took the crumbs from A.

flow.parent: Each crumb should be small enough for one small ant to carry, about the size of a sesame seed. Fresh grated coconut works well in most homes.
flow.context: In this step of the Clean-up Count you set out two papers of crumbs: one for the ants and one that ants cannot reach.

flow.do: Every 5 minutes for 40 minutes, count the ants on paper A and the crumbs left on it. Write both numbers. Between counts, do something else nearby, such as the term cards.
flow.say: Five minutes have passed. Count the ants on the paper, then the crumbs. Write both. Watch one ant closely. Where does she go with her crumb?
flow.kid: Every 5 minutes, count the ants and the crumbs. Write both numbers.
flow.parent: If no ant has found paper A after 15 minutes, slide it to a hand's width from the ant line. Then start the clock again. Some kinds of ant eat at the paper and carry little away. Then the count of ants is your main result. If crumbs are still left after 40 minutes, go on counting for another 20 minutes.
flow.context: In this step of the Clean-up Count you count the ants and the crumbs on paper A every 5 minutes.

flow.do: At the end, count the crumbs on paper B. Write the number in the table.
flow.say: Now count the crumbs on paper B, the one in the water. How many are left? What does that tell us about paper A?
flow.kid: Count the crumbs on paper B. Are all 20 still there?

check.q: In the Clean-up Count, paper B still has 20 crumbs. What does that show?
options: Ants removed the crumbs from paper A
check.why: Paper B had the same crumbs in the same room, and ants could not reach it. All 20 stayed. So the crumbs on paper A did not vanish by themselves: the ants took them.

flow.context: In this step of the Clean-up Count you check the paper that ants could not reach.

flow.do: Draw a line graph. Put minutes along the bottom, from 0 to 40. Put crumbs left up the side, from 0 to 20. Mark a dot for each count and join the dots.
flow.say: Put a dot for each count and join the dots. Look at the shape of the line. Where is it flat? Where is it steepest?
flow.kid: Graph the crumbs left, or tell your grown-up when they went fastest.
flow.parent: A steep part of the line means crumbs were going fast. A flat part means few crumbs were going.
flow.context: In this step of the Clean-up Count you draw a line graph of the crumbs left on paper A.

flow.do: Look at the table and the graph together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Then say why you think it happened. When were the most ants on the paper? When did the crumbs go fastest?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Why did the crumbs go slowly at first and faster later?
good: At first only one ant knew about the food.
She brought more ants, so more crumbs were carried at once.

ask.q: Where are the 20 crumbs now, and what will happen to them?
good: In the nest. The workers will feed them to the larvae.
What is left over will go on the nest's rubbish heap.

flow.parent: In most homes the first ant arrives within 10 minutes, and the crumbs are gone within 30 to 60 minutes. The usual pattern is a slow start and then a rush. The reason: one worker finds the food and goes home, leaving a scent trail. Other workers follow the trail, and each of them strengthens it. So the number of ants at the food grows, and the crumbs go faster. The crumbs are carried into the nest and fed to the larvae. This is recycling: food that fell on your floor becomes new ants, and the leftovers go into the soil. Brush the remaining crumbs outside when you finish.
flow.think: Nobody asked the ants to clean your floor. Why did they do it?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Clean-up Count. You say what your counts and your graph show about how ants clear food.

activities.title: The Kitchen Shelf Test: which foods needed an insect?

materials.item: twelve foods from your kitchen. Six of them: rice, wheat atta, ragi or maize, jaggery or sugar, a banana and a potato
the other six: mustard seeds, coriander seeds, cardamom, a gourd such as pumpkin or cucumber, mango or mango pickle, and coffee or chocolate
two sheets of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Sort twelve kitchen foods by whether an insect was needed to grow them.

activities.record: Two lists: 'An insect was needed' and 'No insect was needed'. Put a star next to each food that you guessed right.
activities.context: In this activity you take twelve foods from your kitchen. You guess which of them could not have grown without an insect pollinator, and then you check. You will find out how many foods on your shelf need insects.

setup.art: Twelve foods in small steel katoris and on a plate on a kitchen counter: rice, atta, ragi, jaggery, a banana, a potato, mustard seeds, coriander seeds, cardamom pods, a slice of pumpkin, a mango and coffee powder.
setup.caption: 1. Put twelve foods on the counter.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper on the counter, one headed 'An insect was needed' and one headed 'No insect was needed', with a child moving a katori of mustard seeds onto the first sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Guess first. Put each food on one of the two sheets.

setup.art: A parent reading from a phone while the child moves a banana from one sheet to the other.
setup.caption: 3. Check each food against the answer list. Move the ones that were wrong.

flow.do: Put the twelve foods on the counter. If one is missing, write its name on a slip of paper. Label the two sheets 'An insect was needed' and 'No insect was needed'.
flow.say: Some of these foods grew only because an insect carried pollen to a flower. Others needed no insect at all. Before we check, which do you think needed an insect? Why?
flow.kid: Look at twelve foods. Which ones needed an insect to grow? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Shelf Test. You set out twelve foods and get ready to guess.

flow.do: Your child puts each food on one of the two sheets and gives a reason. Do not help yet.
flow.say: Put each food on a sheet. Tell me your reason each time. I will not say yet whether you are right.
flow.kid: Put each food on a sheet. Say your reason for each one.

ask.q: What made you put that food on the insect sheet?
good: It is a fruit, and fruits come from flowers.
It is a seed, so a flower must have been pollinated.
I have seen bees on that plant.

flow.parent: Many children put all the plants on one sheet. That is a fine first guess. The checking step shows which plants use wind, and which grow with no pollination.
flow.context: In this step of the Kitchen Shelf Test you sort twelve foods by your own guess.

flow.do: Read the answer list in the note below, one food at a time. Your child moves any food that was on the wrong sheet and puts a star by each right guess.
flow.say: Let us check them one at a time. Rice first. Rice is a grass, and the wind carries its pollen. So rice needed no insect. Were you right?
flow.kid: Check each food with a grown-up. Move the ones that were wrong.

ask.q: What do the foods on the 'no insect' sheet have in common?
good: Many are grains from grasses, and wind carries their pollen.
Some are grown from pieces of the plant, like potato and sugarcane.

flow.parent: No insect was needed: rice, wheat, ragi and maize are grasses, and wind carries their pollen. Sugarcane is a grass grown from pieces of stem. The bananas we eat form with no pollination, which is why they have no hard seeds. Potatoes are grown from pieces of potato. An insect was needed: mustard and coriander seeds form after bees and flies visit the flowers. Cardamom needs bees. Pumpkins and cucumbers have separate pollen flowers and fruit flowers, so an insect must carry pollen between them. Mango flowers are pollinated mostly by flies and small bees. Coffee gives more beans with bees, and cocoa needs tiny flies called midges.

check.q: Why does a rice plant need no insect to make grains?
check.why: Rice is a grass. Rice plants have small plain flowers, and the wind carries their light pollen. If you chose 'no flowers', remember that every grain began as a tiny flower.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Kitchen Shelf Test. You check your guesses and find which foods needed an insect.

activities.title: The Raisin at the Bottom: what does a flower visitor carry away?

materials.item: tall steel tumblers
raisins, or small pieces of jaggery
cotton buds
haldi (turmeric) powder, half a teaspoon in a katori
a strip of white paper about 4 centimetres wide and 25 centimetres long, and sticky tape
an old newspaper to work on

activities.safety: Haldi stains cloth. Work on newspaper, wear old clothes and wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Fetch a raisin from two tumbler flowers and see what your hand carries between them.

activities.record: A photo or a drawing of your hand after flower 1, and of the paper collar of flower 2 after your visit. Show the yellow marks.
activities.context: In this activity two steel tumblers are two flowers, and a raisin at the bottom is the nectar. You fetch the raisins as a bee would, and see what your hand carries from one flower to the other.

setup.art: A steel tumbler with four cotton buds taped to its rim so that their yellow haldi-covered heads lean in over the mouth, and a raisin at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Flower 1: tape four haldi-covered cotton buds to the rim, pointing inwards. Drop in a raisin.

setup.art: A second steel tumbler with a clean white paper collar taped around the inside of its rim, and a raisin at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Flower 2: tape a white paper collar inside the rim. Drop in a raisin.

setup.art: A child's hand reaching into the first tumbler past the yellow cotton buds, with yellow streaks on the back of the hand.
setup.caption: 3. Reach into flower 1 and take the raisin. Look at your hand.

setup.art: The white paper collar of the second tumbler streaked with yellow where the child's hand has passed.
setup.caption: 4. Reach into flower 2 with the same hand. Look at the collar.

flow.do: Roll the four cotton buds in haldi. Tape them to the rim of tumbler 1 with their yellow heads leaning in over the mouth. Tape the white paper strip inside the rim of tumbler 2 as a collar. Drop one raisin into each tumbler.
flow.say: These tumblers are two flowers of the same kind. The raisin is the nectar. The yellow cotton buds on flower 1 are the anthers, and they hold the pollen. The white collar on flower 2 is the stigma.
flow.kid: Make two tumbler flowers. One has yellow anthers. One has a white collar.
flow.parent: The cotton heads should lean in far enough that a hand must brush past them. Place the tumblers about one metre apart on the newspaper.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Raisin at the Bottom. You build two tumbler flowers, one with haldi pollen and one with a clean white collar.

flow.do: Ask for a guess. Then your child reaches into flower 1 with one hand, takes the raisin and looks at the hand.
flow.say: You are a bee, and you want only the raisin. What do you think will happen to your hand? Now reach in and take it.
flow.kid: You are a bee. Reach into flower 1 for the raisin. Look at your hand.

ask.q: You only wanted the raisin. What else did you get?
good: Haldi on my hand.
Pollen, though I was not trying to take any.

flow.context: In this step of the Raisin at the Bottom you fetch the raisin from the flower with haldi pollen.

flow.do: Without wiping the hand, your child reaches into flower 2 for the second raisin. Look at the white collar together. Your child points to the yellow on the hand and on the collar, or takes a photo of each. Then both wash hands and eat the raisins.
flow.say: Do not wipe your hand. Fly to flower 2 and take the raisin. Now look at the white collar. What is on it?
flow.kid: Do not wipe your hand. Take the raisin from flower 2. Look at the collar.

check.q: In the Raisin at the Bottom, how did haldi reach the white collar of flower 2?
options: On the hand that fetched the raisins
It blew across in the air
It was on the second raisin
check.why: The hand brushed the yellow cotton buds in flower 1 and then brushed the collar in flower 2. A bee pollinates in the same way, while she is fetching nectar.

flow.parent: This is the heart of pollination. The visitor comes for food. The flower places its anthers and its stigma where the visitor must brush past them.
flow.think: Why does a real flower keep its nectar at the very bottom?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Raisin at the Bottom. You visit the second flower and see what your hand left on its white collar.

activities.title: From One Queen: draw the first year of an ant colony

materials.item: a sheet of plain paper, a ruler, a pencil and colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw six boxes that show how one queen ant becomes a colony.

activities.record: A strip of six boxes, each with a drawing and one line of writing. Under the strip, write one question that you still have.
activities.context: In this activity you draw six boxes in a row. They show how one queen ant starts a colony alone, and how the colony grows in a year.

setup.art: A sheet of paper turned sideways and ruled into six boxes in a row, numbered 1 to 6.
setup.caption: 1. Rule six boxes in a row and number them.

setup.art: The first three boxes filled in: winged ants flying in rain, a queen with broken-off wings digging, and the queen in a sealed hole with eggs.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one stage in each box, as a grown-up reads it out.

setup.art: All six boxes filled in, the last showing a large nest with many ants and a few winged ones at the entrance, with a line of writing under each box.
setup.caption: 3. Write one line under each box.

flow.do: Rule six boxes in a row across the paper. Number them 1 to 6.
flow.say: Every ant colony in the world was started by one queen. Before I read the stages, how do you think she begins? Who feeds her first young?
flow.kid: Rule six boxes. How do you think one ant starts a colony?
flow.context: This is the first step of From One Queen. You rule six boxes and guess how a colony begins.

flow.do: Read the six stages in the note below, one at a time. Your child shows each stage in its box. They can draw it quickly or use small things, such as a crumb. They say one line. Write it under the box.
flow.say: Here is stage one. Listen, then show it in box 1 and tell me one line. Tell me when you are ready for the next stage.
flow.kid: Listen to each stage. Show it in a box. Say one line.
flow.parent: Stage 1: after the first heavy rain, winged young queens and males fly out of many nests and mate in the air. Stage 2: a mated queen lands, breaks off her wings and digs a small hole. Stage 3: she seals the hole and lays her first eggs. Stage 4: she eats nothing for weeks, and feeds the first larvae from her own body. Stage 5: the first small workers grow up, open the nest and bring food home. Stage 6: after a year there are hundreds of workers. After some years the colony raises its own winged queens and males.
flow.context: In this step of From One Queen you draw the six stages of a new ant colony.

flow.do: Look at the strip together. Ask the questions below. Your child writes one question of their own under the strip.
flow.say: Look at box 4 and box 5. Who helps the queen now? What question do you still have about her?
flow.kid: Look at your six boxes. Point to the box where the first workers appear.

ask.q: What changes for the queen when the first workers grow up?
good: She stops doing everything herself.
The workers bring food, and she only lays eggs.

check.q: How does a queen ant feed her very first larvae?
check.why: She is sealed in alone, and no workers exist yet. She uses up her own body, above all the wing muscles she no longer needs. If you chose 'workers', remember that the first workers are those very larvae.

flow.context: This is the last step of From One Queen. You look at your drawing and say what changes when the first workers grow up.

activities.title: Jumping Pollen: can pollen cross a gap without being touched?

materials.item: a plastic comb or a plastic ruler
a pinch of haldi powder and a few bits of tissue paper, each smaller than a grain of rice
a steel plate, and your own dry hair or a woollen or polyester cloth

schedule.what: Rub a plastic comb and see whether haldi and paper bits jump up to it.

activities.record: Two lines: what happened with the comb before rubbing, and what happened after rubbing.
activities.context: In this activity you rub a plastic comb and hold it above a pinch of haldi. A flying bee carries a small electric charge, and you test whether a charge can make powder jump.

setup.art: A steel plate with a small pinch of yellow haldi powder and a few tiny bits of tissue paper on it.
setup.caption: 1. Put a pinch of haldi and a few bits of tissue paper on a plate.

setup.art: A child running a plastic comb through her dry hair.
setup.caption: 2. Rub the comb through dry hair ten times.

setup.art: The comb held a finger's width above the plate, with paper bits and yellow specks clinging to its teeth.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the comb just above the haldi, without touching. Watch closely.

flow.do: Put the haldi and paper bits on the plate. Your child holds the comb 1 centimetre above them, before rubbing it. Ask what they see. Then ask for a guess about the rubbed comb.
flow.say: Hold the comb just above the haldi. Does anything move? Now we will rub the comb through your hair. What do you think will happen then? Why?
flow.kid: Hold the comb above the haldi. Does anything move? Guess what rubbing will do.
flow.context: This is the first step of Jumping Pollen. You hold a comb above haldi before rubbing it, and guess what rubbing will change.

flow.do: Your child rubs the comb through dry hair ten times, or rubs it hard on the cloth. They hold it 1 centimetre above the haldi and the paper bits at once.
flow.say: Rub ten times, then hold the comb close at once. Do not touch the powder. Look along the teeth of the comb.
flow.kid: Rub the comb ten times. Hold it just above the haldi. Look closely.
flow.parent: The paper bits usually jump first, and yellow specks follow. On a damp monsoon day this may fail, because the charge leaks away. Try again in a dry room under a fan, or on another day.
flow.context: In this step of Jumping Pollen you rub the comb and hold it just above the haldi and paper bits.

flow.do: Talk about what happened. Then read the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. The comb never touched the haldi. So how did the haldi reach the comb?
flow.kid: Say what you saw. The comb never touched the haldi.

ask.q: How might this help a bee who lands on a flower?
good: Pollen could jump onto her before she touches it.
She would pick up more pollen.

flow.parent: Rubbing gave the comb an electric charge, and a charged thing attracts light specks. A bee's body picks up a small charge as she flies through the air. Scientists have filmed pollen jumping a gap of a few millimetres onto a bee. In 2013 a team in Britain also showed that bumblebees can sense the electric charge of a flower.
flow.context: This is the last step of Jumping Pollen. You say how the haldi reached the comb, and what this means for a bee.

projects.title: A Flower Calendar for Our Street: three days

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a large sheet of paper or the back of an old calendar, and colour pencils
an older neighbour, a grandparent, a gardener or a flower seller to ask

schedule.what: List every tree and plant you can see from your home or on your way to the shop.
Ask an elder in which months each one flowers. Watch one flowering plant for five minutes.
Draw the calendar and find the hungry months.

projects.record: A chart with the twelve months across the top and one row for each plant. Colour the months in which that plant flowers. Circle any month with no flowers at all.
projects.context: In this three-day project you find out in which months the trees and plants near your home flower. A bee colony needs flowers all year, and your calendar shows the months when bees near you go hungry.

setup.art: A child at a balcony railing writing a list, looking at a street with a neem tree, a coconut palm, a drumstick tree and a pot of tulsi.
setup.caption: 1. List the trees and plants near your home.

setup.art: A child with a notebook talking to an old woman who is pointing up at a flowering tree.
setup.caption: 2. Ask an elder when each one flowers.

setup.art: A large chart with twelve month columns and rows for different plants, with coloured bars in some months and one empty month circled in red.
setup.caption: 3. Colour the flowering months. Circle the months with no flowers.

flow.do: Day 1. Look out of every window, and look around on your way to the shop. List up to ten trees and plants. Balcony pots count. If your child does not know a name, they pick up one fallen leaf or take a photo of the plant.
flow.say: A bee colony must find flowers in every month, or the bees go hungry. Let us list the plants near us that could feed them. Which ones have you seen in flower?
flow.kid: List ten trees and plants near your home. If you lack a name, take a photo or a leaf.
flow.parent: Common city trees that feed bees well are neem, drumstick, coconut, tamarind, jamun, gulmohar and copper pod. Tulsi, curry leaf and coriander left to flower feed them too. You need no garden for this project.
flow.context: This is day 1 of A Flower Calendar for Our Street. You list the trees and plants near your home.

flow.do: Day 2. Take the list to an elder, a gardener or a flower seller. Ask in which months each plant flowers, and write the months. If one plant is in flower now and within reach, watch it for five minutes and count the visitors.
flow.say: Ask your questions and write down the months. People who have lived here for years know this better than any book. Then let us watch one plant in flower, if we can reach one.
flow.kid: Ask an elder when each plant flowers. Write the months. Watch one flower.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you make the list
flow.parent: If no elder knows a plant, write 'not sure' and leave that row pale. If nothing is in flower, skip the watching. The calendar still works.
flow.context: This is day 2 of A Flower Calendar for Our Street. You ask an elder when each plant flowers.

flow.do: Day 3. Draw the chart: twelve months across the top and one row for each plant. Colour the flowering months. Count the plants in flower in each month and write the number at the bottom.
flow.say: Colour each plant's flowering months. Now count down each column. Which month has the most flowers? Is there a month with none? What could a family grow to fill that month?
flow.kid: Colour the flowering months. Which month has the fewest flowers?
flow.wait: Do this the day after you ask the elder

ask.q: What happens to a bee colony in a month with no flowers?
good: The bees live on their stored honey.
If the store runs out, the colony goes hungry or moves away.

flow.think: Which one plant could your family grow to feed bees in the hungry month?
flow.context: This is day 3 of A Flower Calendar for Our Street. You draw the calendar and find the months with few flowers.

challenges.title: The Buzz Flower: get the pollen out of a closed tube
challenges.problem: A brinjal flower keeps its pollen inside closed tubes with one small hole at the tip. A honeybee cannot get the pollen out. A carpenter bee shakes the pollen out by buzzing. Your problem is like hers. A paper tube holds haldi and has one small hole. Get out as much haldi as you can in 10 seconds.
constraints: Do not squeeze, tear or open the tube.
Do not make the hole bigger.
Hold the tube with the hole pointing down, over a steel plate.
Each method gets 10 seconds, counted aloud.
Refill the tube to the same level before each method.
materials: a square of notebook paper, 8 centimetres wide, and sticky tape
a pencil to roll the tube around
haldi powder mixed with the same amount of atta, 2 teaspoons in all
a steel plate to catch the powder
a phone that can be set to vibrate
a rubber band and a steel tumbler
an old newspaper to work on
general: Flick the side of the tube with a finger.
Shake the tube up and down.
Knock the tube gently against the edge of the plate.
creative: Hold the tube against a phone while it vibrates.
Stretch a rubber band over a steel tumbler, rest the tube on the band and pluck the band.
Press the tube lightly against your throat and hum a low, loud note.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to shake the tube. It must leave the tube whole. Test it for 10 seconds and compare the heap with your best heap so far. Show your method to a grown-up, or draw it, and say why you think it worked or failed.
challenges.context: In this challenge you must get haldi out of a paper tube through one small hole. You may not squeeze or open the tube. It is the problem a carpenter bee solves on a brinjal flower.

setup.art: A small paper tube rolled around a pencil and taped, with one end folded over and taped shut.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the paper around a pencil and tape it. Fold one end shut and tape it.

setup.art: The tube half filled with yellow powder, its open end closed with tape that has a small hole pushed through with a pencil tip.
setup.caption: 2. Half fill the tube with the haldi mix. Tape the end and push one small hole with a pencil tip.

setup.art: A child holding the tube hole-down over a steel plate and flicking it with a finger, with a small yellow heap on the plate.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the tube hole-down over a plate. Try one method for 10 seconds.

setup.art: A steel plate with four small yellow heaps of different sizes, each beside a paper label naming a method.
setup.caption: 4. Make a new heap for each method. Compare the heaps.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Build the tube as the steps show. Hold it hole-down over the plate without moving, and count to 10.
flow.say: This tube is the pollen tube of a brinjal flower. Hold it still with the hole down. Does the powder pour out? What could a bee do to get the powder out?
flow.kid: Build the tube. Hold it hole-down and count to 10.

ask.q: The hole is open, so why does the powder stay inside?
good: The powder sticks to itself and blocks the hole.
Nothing is shaking it loose.

flow.parent: The hole should be about as wide as a pencil tip. With atta mixed in, the powder clumps and hardly falls while the tube is still. If it pours out freely, make a new tube with a smaller hole.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Buzz Flower. You build a paper tube of haldi and find that the powder stays in while the tube is still.

flow.do: Try the three usual methods, 10 seconds each. Refill the tube before each. Make a separate heap on the plate for each method and label the heaps.
flow.say: Try a flick, then a shake, then a knock. Count ten seconds for each. Keep the heaps apart, so that we can compare them.
flow.kid: Try a flick, a shake and a knock. Make one heap for each.
flow.context: In this step of the Buzz Flower you try three usual ways of shaking the haldi out of the tube.

flow.do: Try the creative methods. Set the phone to vibrate and hold the tube against it. Try the rubber band, and try humming. Make a heap for each.
flow.say: A carpenter bee does not flick the flower. She buzzes her flight muscles a few hundred times each second. Which of our methods is most like her buzz? Let us test it.
flow.kid: Now try a buzzing phone, a plucked rubber band and a hum.
flow.parent: Fast, small shakes often free more powder than slow, big ones. Results vary with the tube and the phone, so let the heaps decide.
flow.context: In this step of the Buzz Flower you try fast vibrations, as a carpenter bee does.

flow.do: Compare all the heaps. Your child invents one more method and tests it. They draw it or show it to you.
flow.say: Which heap is biggest? Was a fast, small shake better than a slow, big one? Now invent your own method and test it.
flow.kid: Which heap is biggest? Invent your own method and test it.

check.q: Why can a carpenter bee get pollen from a brinjal flower when a honeybee cannot?
options: She shakes the flower by buzzing
check.why: Brinjal pollen sits in closed tubes with a small hole. A carpenter bee grips the flower and buzzes, and the shaking throws the pollen out. Honeybees do not buzz flowers in this way.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Buzz Flower. You compare the heaps of haldi and invent your own way to shake the tube.

items.p: Who lays the eggs in a honeybee colony?
items.why: The queen is the mother of the colony, and laying eggs is her work. Drones are males who only mate. Larvae are the young.

items.p: The worker ants in one line on a wall are mostly what to each other?
items.why: Workers are daughters of the same queen, so they are sisters. If you chose brothers, remember that worker ants are female.

items.p: The moving of pollen from an anther to a stigma is called ____.
items.why: Pollination must happen before a flower can grow seeds and fruit.

items.p: The sweet liquid that flowers make, and that insects drink for energy, is called ____.
items.why: Nectar is mostly sugar and water. Honeybees dry it into honey.

items.p: All the worker bees in a hive are female.
items.why: True. Workers are daughters of the queen. The few males are called drones, and they do no nest work.

items.p: Rice needs bees to carry its pollen.
items.why: False. Rice is a grass, and the wind carries its pollen. Rice, wheat and maize need no insect.

items.p: Match each part of a flower to what it does.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The anther and the stigma do the work of making seeds. The nectar and the petals bring the insect who carries the pollen between them.

items.p: Sort these foods. Did the plant need an insect pollinator, or not?
items.a: see items
items.why: Rice and wheat are grasses, and wind carries their pollen. The bananas we eat form with no pollination, and potatoes grow from pieces of potato. The other four set fruit or seed after insects visit.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how a queen ant starts a colony.
items: She flies out after rain and mates
She lands and breaks off her wings
She digs a hole and seals herself in
She lays eggs and feeds the first larvae from her own body
Her first daughters open the nest and bring food
a: She flies out after rain and mates
She lands and breaks off her wings
She digs a hole and seals herself in
She lays eggs and feeds the first larvae from her own body
Her first daughters open the nest and bring food
items.why: The queen does everything alone until her first daughters grow up. After that the workers feed her, and she only lays eggs.

items.p: In the Hairy or Smooth test, why did each carrier get three rows of boxes?
opts: One try can be a fluke
Because an insect has three body parts
items.why: One row might come out odd by chance. If three rows give similar counts, the result can be trusted more.

items.p: Which insect's young clear away dead animals?
items.why: A blowfly lays eggs on a dead body, and her maggots eat the body. Young honeybees eat pollen and honey, and caterpillars eat leaves.

items.p: What does a worker bee carry home in the baskets on her back legs?
items.why: She packs pollen into baskets of stiff hairs on her back legs. Pollen is the protein food that makes larvae grow. Nectar is carried inside her body.

items.p: Explain in two sentences how a bee pollinates a pumpkin flower while she collects food.
items.a: The bee crawls into a pumpkin flower for nectar, and pollen from the anthers sticks to her hairs. At the next pumpkin flower some of that pollen rubs off on the sticky stigma.
items.why: A strong answer says three things. The bee comes for food, pollen sticks to her body, and the pollen rubs off on another flower's stigma.

items.p: In the Clean-up Count, paper B stood on a katori in water. Explain what paper B was for.
items.a: Ants could not cross the water, so paper B had crumbs and no ants. It kept all its crumbs. That showed the ants took the crumbs from paper A.
items.why: A strong answer says that paper B shows what happens with no ants. Then the ants are the only difference between the two papers.

items.p: Draw a bee visiting two flowers. Use arrows to show where pollen is picked up and where it is left.
items.a: Two flowers of the same kind with a bee between them. One arrow goes from the anthers of the first flower to the bee, labelled 'picked up'. One arrow goes from the bee to the stigma of the second flower, labelled 'left here'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows pollen leaving an anther and arriving on a stigma. The bee is the carrier in between.
items.art: A blank box with the outlines of two open flowers and a bee between them.

items.p: Sort these animals into 'insect' and 'not an insect'. Count the legs to help you.
items.a: see items
items.why: Insects have six legs. Spiders and scorpions have eight legs, so they are not insects.

worksheets.title: Why insects are good at this work

items.p: Why does a hairy insect carry more pollen than a smooth one?
items.why: Pollen grains are held in the gaps between hairs and come off a little at a time. A smooth body holds pollen only on its surface.

items.p: A bee visits twenty sunflowers in a row and no other flower. What is this habit called?
items.why: Flower constancy means keeping to one kind of flower on one trip. It takes sunflower pollen to sunflowers, where it can work.

items.p: A brinjal flower keeps its pollen in closed tubes. Which visitor can shake it out?
items.why: A carpenter bee grips the flower and buzzes, and the shaking throws the pollen out. Honeybees, butterflies and ants do not buzz flowers.

items.p: A worker bee lives about six weeks. Why is her colony still there a year later?
opts: The queen does all the work
items.why: The queen lays eggs every day in the warm months, and new workers replace those who die. The colony goes on while its members change.

items.p: Termites are a kind of ant.
items.why: False. Termites are close relatives of cockroaches. Ants are close relatives of wasps and bees. A termite colony has a king as well as a queen.

items.p: A flower gains when a bee keeps to one kind of flower on a trip.
items.why: True. Pollen works only on a flower of the same kind. A bee who mixes flowers wastes most of the pollen she carries.

items.p: Sort these insects by the work they are doing.
items: a carpenter bee buzzing on a brinjal flower
a hawkmoth drinking at a jasmine flower
a midge inside a cocoa flower
a termite chewing a dead branch
a maggot eating a dead fish
items.a: see items
items.why: An insect feeding at a flower is likely to be moving pollen. An insect eating dung, dead wood or a dead animal is breaking that material down. Then the material can be used again.

items.p: Three of these plants are pollinated by wind. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Rice, wheat and maize are grasses with light pollen that the wind carries. Mango flowers are pollinated by flies and small bees.

items.p: In the Hairy or Smooth test, a cotton bud marked 12, 10 and 14 boxes. What is the middle value?
items.why: Put the three numbers in order: 10, 12, 14. The middle one is 12. The middle value is not pulled about by one odd row.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how ants clear crumbs from a floor.
items: She goes home, leaving a scent trail
More ants follow the trail to the crumbs
The ants carry the crumbs into the nest
Workers feed the crumbs to the larvae
a: She goes home, leaving a scent trail
More ants follow the trail to the crumbs
The ants carry the crumbs into the nest
Workers feed the crumbs to the larvae
items.why: The work starts slowly, with one ant. It speeds up when her nestmates follow her trail. The food ends up inside young ants.

items.p: A mango orchard has thousands of flowers and very few bees. Explain how the flowers can still be pollinated.
items.a: Flies visit mango flowers too. The flowers are small and open, so a fly's short mouth can reach the nectar. Pollen sticks to the fly's bristles and reaches the next flower.
items.why: A strong answer names another pollinator, such as flies, and says why that pollinator suits a small open flower.

items.p: Why does a flower gain by keeping its nectar at the very bottom?
items.a: The insect has to push deep into the flower to reach the nectar. On the way she brushes against the anthers and the stigma, so pollen is picked up and left.
items.why: A strong answer links the place of the nectar to the insect's path past the anthers and the stigma.

items.p: Dung beetles bury cow dung in the ground. Explain two ways in which this helps a field.
items.a: Buried dung feeds the soil near the roots of the grass. The grass under the dung is uncovered and can grow again. The beetles' tunnels also let rain soak in.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different gains. Three possible gains are food for the soil, cleared grass, and tunnels that let in water and air.

items.p: Green flies sit on the mango flowers in an orchard. Three people say what should be done about flies.

views.says: Flies walk on waste and then on food, and they carry germs. They should be killed wherever they are found.
Flies pollinate my mango flowers. With fewer flies I pick fewer mangoes. Nobody should spray them near my trees.
Maggots clear away dead animals, and adult flies pollinate. Keep flies off food with covers and nets, and leave them alone outdoors.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Give a reason from this lesson. Then answer the person you disagree with most.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that flies really do carry germs to uncovered food. Another is that most visitors to mango flowers in many orchards are flies. A third is that maggots clear dead animals in days.
items.why: Each person is right about something. A strong answer uses a fact from the unit and deals fairly with the other side. One fair way is to keep flies off food without killing them everywhere.

items.p: Label three things in this flower: an anther, the stigma, and the place where the nectar is.
a: An anther: one of the small knobs that make pollen
The stigma: the sticky tip that catches pollen
Where the nectar is: at the bottom of the flower, at the base of the petals
items.why: The nectar is deepest. So a visitor passes the anthers and the stigma on the way down and on the way out.
items.art: A large open flower cut in half, showing several knobbed anthers, one central stalk with a sticky tip, and a small drop at the base, with three blank label lines.

items.p: Every insect has wings.
items.why: False. Flies and grasshoppers have wings, but worker ants have none. Insects are the animals with six legs and one pair of antennae.

items.p: Match each animal to how it uses a mango tree.
pairs: stitch a nest from the leaves
builds a nest in the branches
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A tree can shelter some animals and feed others. Weaver ants and crows use it as a home, and a honeybee uses its flowers for food.

items.p: A farmer ties fine net bags over some of her pumpkin flowers. What is she testing?
opts: Whether insects are needed for fruit
items.why: A fine net keeps insects out and lets in light and air. If the bagged flowers make no pumpkins and the open ones do, insects were needed.

items.p: Most kinds of crop gain from pollinators, but most food by weight does not. Why?
opts: People eat huge amounts of wind-pollinated grains
Insects eat most of the fruit
items.why: Rice, wheat and maize are only three kinds of crop, but people eat them in enormous amounts. So a count by kind and a count by weight give different answers.

items.p: In the Clean-up Count, a graph of crumbs left stays flat for 5 minutes. What does the flat part show?
opts: No ant had taken a crumb yet
items.why: A flat line means the number of crumbs did not change. At the start, no ant has found the food, or one ant has only just arrived.

items.p: A huge field grows one crop that flowers for two weeks. What problem does a bee colony face there?
opts: No flowers for the rest of the year
items.why: A colony must eat in every month. After the two weeks of flowers, the bees find nothing nearby. Mixed plants that flower at different times feed them all year.

items.p: If all bees vanished, humans would have no food at all.
items.why: False. Rice, wheat, maize, potatoes and bananas need no insect pollinator. People would lose many fruits, nuts, vegetables and spices, and the diet would be much poorer.

items.p: One kind of fly can be a recycler when young and a pollinator when grown.
items.why: True. Blowfly maggots eat dead animals. The adult flies drink nectar and carry pollen on their bristles.

items.p: Match each pollinator to the flower she suits best.
pairs: Brinjal flower with pollen in closed tubes
Pale, scented flower that opens at night
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A flower's shape, scent and opening time fit the bodies and habits of some visitors and not others. A buzzing bee, a night flier, a short mouth and a tiny body each suit a different flower.

items.p: A queen honeybee lays 1,000 eggs a day. How many eggs does she lay in 30 days?
items.why: 1,000 times 30 is 30,000. This is how a colony can replace its workers, who live only about six weeks in summer.

items.p: A group of animals that lives so closely together that the group behaves like one body is called a ____.
items.why: William Morton Wheeler wrote in 1911 that an ant colony is like one living body. Scientists still argue about whether this is the best way to see a colony.

items.p: A spray kills the insects who are eating a crop. Give two reasons why the harvest might still fall.
items.a: The spray also kills the bees and flies who pollinate the crop, so fewer fruits form. It also kills the insects who hunt the crop-eaters, so the crop-eaters can come back in greater numbers.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different effects: the loss of pollinators, and the loss of the hunters that keep crop-eating insects in check.

items.p: Plan a fair test: do ants clear sweet crumbs faster than salty crumbs? Say what you would keep the same.
items.a: Put 20 sweet crumbs on one paper and 20 salty crumbs on another. Keep the crumb size, the number, the paper and the distance from the ant line the same. Count the crumbs left on each paper every 5 minutes.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the kind of crumb. It keeps the number, the size, the place and the timing the same, and it says what will be counted.

items.p: In a Hairy or Smooth test, a damp pen end marked 9 boxes. Explain why a damp pen spoils the test.
items.a: Wet things pick up far more powder than dry things. So the test would be comparing wet with dry, and not smooth with hairy. Only one thing should differ between the two carriers.
items.why: A strong answer says that dampness is a second difference between the carriers. Then nobody can tell which difference caused the result.

items.p: A worker bee usually has no young of her own. Explain how her work still helps young bees to live.
items.a: She feeds and guards the larvae, who are her sisters. Some of those sisters become new queens and start new colonies. So her family goes on because of her work.
items.why: A strong answer says that the larvae she raises are her own close family. It also says that new queens come from among them.

items.p: A village wants better harvests of pumpkin, mustard and mango. Three people give advice.

views.says: Put bee boxes in the fields. One box brings thousands of pollinators to the right place on the right day.

views.who: A scientist who studies wild bees
views.says: Wild bees and flies already do much of this work, and some do it better. Keep patches of wild flowers and dead wood where they can nest.

views.who: A farmer with a small field
views.says: I cannot pay for boxes or leave land unused. I will stop spraying when the crop is in flower, which costs me nothing.

items.ask: Which advice would you follow first? Give a reason from this lesson. Then say what the other two would add.
items.a: Any choice with a reason. One reason is that a study of 600 fields found wild insects raised harvests in every crop. Another is that mango is pollinated mostly by flies, which no bee box supplies. A third is that spraying on open flowers kills every kind of pollinator.
items.why: All three pieces of advice can work together. A strong answer picks one, supports it with a fact, and sees what the others would add.

items.p: Draw the inside of an ant nest or a honeybee nest. Show and label the queen, workers, larvae and the food store.
items.a: An ant nest has tunnels and rooms in soil. A large queen is in one room, and small white larvae are in a nursery room. Workers carry food, and one room holds stored seeds or dead insects. A honeybee nest is a wax comb with honey cells at the top and larvae in the middle. The long queen and many workers are on the comb.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the nest has different places for different things: young in one part, food in another, and workers moving between them.
items.art: A blank box with a line across the top to show ground level and a small entrance hole.

items.p: Match each crop problem to a way of guarding the crop that does not poison bees.
pairs: Neel gai in a wheat field at night
a fence or a night watch
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each problem has its own answer. Neel gai are large animals, so a fence or a watch works. Caterpillars can be picked off, and sticky cards trap small flying insects. None of these poison bees.

opts: One insect family sharing one nest
Any crowd of insects on a flower
quiz.why: A colony is a family: a queen, her worker daughters and the young, in one nest. Insects who only happen to meet at a flower are not a colony.

quiz.p: What is the queen's main work in a grown colony?
quiz.why: The queen is the mother, and she lays the eggs. She does not give orders. The workers find food, guard the nest and feed her.

quiz.p: How does a new honeybee colony usually begin?
opts: The old queen leaves with a swarm
Eggs blow away on the wind
The drones build a new nest
quiz.why: The old queen flies off with about half the workers, and the bees who stay raise a new queen. A worker alone cannot start a colony.

opts: Pollen moving from an anther to a stigma
A seed falling to the ground
quiz.why: Pollination is the journey of pollen from where it is made to the sticky tip that catches it. Honey-making happens later, in the hive.

quiz.p: Which part of a flower catches pollen?
quiz.why: The stigma is sticky and catches pollen. If you chose the anther, remember that the anther makes pollen and gives it away.

quiz.p: Which result of a Hairy or Smooth test shows that a hairy carrier holds more pollen?
opts: The cotton bud marks far more boxes
Both carriers mark the same number
quiz.why: The cotton bud holds powder between its threads and lets it out box after box. The smooth pen runs out after one or two boxes.

quiz.p: Why does a bee visit a flower?
opts: To collect nectar and pollen as food
To help the flower make seeds
quiz.why: A bee visits flowers to feed herself and her colony. The flower is pollinated because pollen sticks to her and rubs off at the next flower.

quiz.p: Which of these foods needs no insect pollinator?
quiz.why: Rice is a grass, and wind carries its pollen. Mango, pumpkin and cardamom all set fruit after insects visit their flowers.

quiz.p: Honeybees are the only insects that pollinate crops.
quiz.why: False. Carpenter bees, stingless bees, flies, moths, butterflies and beetles all pollinate. Flies are main pollinators of mango, and midges pollinate cocoa.

quiz.p: Which insects turn a dead branch back into soil?
quiz.why: Termites eat dead wood, with the help of microbes and fungi. The other three feed at flowers.

quiz.p: When ants clear crumbs, why do the crumbs go faster after a slow start?
opts: More ants follow the first ant's trail
quiz.why: At first only one ant knows about the food. She leaves a scent trail, more ants follow, and many crumbs are carried at once.

quiz.p: Which of these helps pollinators most?
opts: Never spraying a plant in flower
Keeping bright lights on all night
quiz.why: Insects come to open flowers, so a spray on flowers poisons the very insects the plant needs. The other three all harm pollinators.

quiz.p: Anita counts the legs on a beetle. How many legs does an insect have?
quiz.why: Every insect has six legs, in three pairs. Eight legs belong to a spider, and a spider is not an insect.

quiz.p: What do the weaver ants and the crow in a mango tree both get from the tree?
opts: A place to live and be safe
quiz.why: A tree gives shelter. The ants stitch nests in the leaves, and the crow builds in the branches. The ants do not eat pollen from the tree, and wax comb is made by honeybees.

quiz.p: A farmer finds caterpillars on her cabbage. Which choice is safest for bees?
opts: Spraying a strong poison on the open flowers
Picking the caterpillars off by hand
Spraying neem on the flowers at noon
quiz.why: Picking by hand harms no bee. A strong poison on open flowers kills bees. Even neem should go only on leaves, in the evening, when bees are not there.

applications: Apple growers in Himachal Pradesh and Kashmir rent bee boxes when their trees flower. More flowers are pollinated, so more apples form.
Beekeepers in India move their bee boxes with the seasons. Many take them to the mustard fields of Rajasthan in winter and to the litchi orchards of Bihar in spring.
Tomato growers with greenhouses keep boxes of bumblebees. Bumblebees buzz the pollen out of tomato flowers, which honeybees cannot do.
Vanilla has no natural pollinator in India. Workers pollinate every vanilla flower by hand with a thin stick.
Some cities and farms feed kitchen waste to the larvae of the black soldier fly. The larvae turn the waste into compost, and they are then fed to hens and fish.
Fruit growers in parts of Asia keep weaver ant nests in their trees. The ants hunt the insects who eat the fruit, so less poison is needed.
Doctors sometimes put clean, specially raised maggots on a wound that will not heal. The maggots eat the dead flesh and leave the living flesh.
Engineers copy the six-sided cells of a honeycomb to make panels for aircraft. The panels are light and very stiff.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of insect are there?
open_questions.why_open: About one million kinds have been named. Estimates of the real number run to five million or more. Most kinds have never been studied by anyone.

open_questions.q: Are insects becoming fewer everywhere, or only in some places?
open_questions.why_open: Long counts exist mainly from Europe and North America, and many of them show steep falls. There are very few long counts from India, Africa or South America.

open_questions.q: Why do some honeybee colonies suddenly lose nearly all their workers?
open_questions.why_open: From 2006, beekeepers in several countries found hives with a queen and young but almost no workers. Poisons, mites, diseases and poor food are all suspected. No single cause has been proved.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a bee?
open_questions.why_open: Bees sense, learn, remember and choose. In a 2022 study, bumblebees rolled small wooden balls again and again for no reward, which looks like play. Nobody has yet found a way to learn what this is like for the bee.

open_questions.q: How does a colony decide when to split and send out a swarm?
open_questions.why_open: Crowding, the age of the queen and the season all play a part. How thousands of workers reach that one decision together is still being worked out.
