maths.problem: In a Hairy or Smooth test, the cotton bud marked 12, 10 and 14 boxes. The pen marked 2, 3 and 1 boxes. Find the middle value for each carrier. How many times as many boxes did the cotton bud mark?
maths.answer: The middle values are 12 and 2. The cotton bud marked 6 times as many boxes.
maths.explain: In order, the cotton bud's counts are 10, 12, 14, and the middle one is 12. The pen's counts are 1, 2, 3, and the middle one is 2. 12 divided by 2 is 6.
maths.context: In the Hairy or Smooth test you carry haldi along rows of 15 paper boxes. You use a cotton bud and a smooth pen end. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: One row can come out odd. The middle value of three rows gives a fairer number, and dividing shows how large the difference is.

maths.problem: In a Clean-up Count, the crumbs left were counted every 5 minutes. The counts were 20, 20, 19, 17, 13, 7, 2 and 0. In which 5 minutes did the ants take the most crumbs? Why not in the first 5 minutes?
maths.answer: Between 20 and 25 minutes, when 6 crumbs went. In the first 5 minutes no ant had brought her nestmates yet.
maths.explain: Take each count from the one before it. The drops are 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 5 and 2. The biggest drop is 6, from 13 to 7. That is the fifth drop, between 20 and 25 minutes. Early on, only one ant knew about the crumbs.
maths.context: In the Clean-up Count you put 20 crumbs near an ant line and count the crumbs left every 5 minutes. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: The size of each drop shows how fast the ants were working at that time. The last number alone would hide the slow start and the rush.

maths.problem: In the Kitchen Shelf Test, 6 of the 12 foods needed an insect. In one month a family eats 18 kilograms of rice, atta and potatoes. They also eat 6 kilograms of foods that needed insects. What fraction of the food by weight needed insects? Why is it not one half?
maths.answer: One quarter by weight. It is less than one half because the family eats large amounts of a few foods that need no insect.
maths.explain: 18 plus 6 is 24 kilograms in all. 6 out of 24 is one quarter. Counted by kind, half the foods needed insects. Counted by weight, only a quarter did, because rice and atta are eaten every day in large amounts.
maths.context: In the Kitchen Shelf Test you sort twelve kitchen foods by whether an insect pollinator was needed. The weights here are made up.
maths.why_maths: A fraction by kind and a fraction by weight answer different questions. Working out both explains two true statements about one world: 'three quarters of crops' and 'one third of food'.

maths.problem: A honeybee may visit about 100 flowers on one trip, and make about 10 trips in a day. About how many flowers does she visit in a day? A colony sends out 10,000 such bees. About how many flower visits is that in one day?
maths.answer: About 1,000 flowers for one bee. About 10,000,000 visits for the colony, which is ten million.
maths.explain: 100 times 10 is 1,000. Then 1,000 times 10,000 is 10,000,000. These are rough numbers, and they change with the weather and the flowers.
maths.context: In the Raisin at the Bottom you visited two tumbler flowers and carried haldi between them. A real bee visits far more flowers than two.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows why one colony can pollinate a whole orchard. No single visit matters much, but ten million visits a day do.

maths.problem: A honeybee colony in summer has 42,000 workers. Each worker lives about 42 days. About how many workers die each day? About how many eggs must the queen lay each day to keep the colony the same size?
maths.answer: About 1,000 workers die each day. So the queen must lay about 1,000 eggs a day.
maths.explain: If 42,000 workers are replaced over 42 days, then 42,000 divided by 42 gives 1,000 a day. To stay the same size, the colony needs 1,000 new workers a day. So the queen must lay at least that many eggs.
maths.context: In From One Queen you drew how one queen ant builds up a colony. This problem asks how a grown honeybee colony stays the same size while its workers keep dying.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows that a colony is rebuilt all the time. It also shows why a queen who stops laying means the end of the colony within weeks.

maths.problem: In Flower Loyal there are 24 cards: 6 each of four kinds of flower. You turn over a pumpkin flower first. How many of the other 23 cards are pumpkin flowers? By luck alone, is your next card likely or unlikely to match?
maths.answer: 5 of the 23 are pumpkin flowers. A match by luck is unlikely: less than 1 chance in 4.
maths.explain: There were 6 pumpkin cards and you hold 1, so 5 are left among 23 cards. 5 out of 23 is a little less than 1 out of 4. So a player who remembers where the pumpkin flowers are does far better than a player who guesses.
maths.context: In the game Flower Loyal you turn over flower cards. You score when you find the same kind of flower again.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the chance of a lucky match shows how much memory adds. A bee who remembers where her flowers grow wastes far fewer visits.

how_we_found_out.story: About 250 years ago, most people who studied plants thought that a flower pollinated itself. Insects on flowers were seen as thieves who stole the nectar. Christian Konrad Sprengel was the head of a school in Spandau, in Germany. In 1787 he looked closely at a wild geranium and saw tiny hairs at the base of each petal. He worked out that the hairs keep rain off the nectar. Then he asked why a flower should protect its nectar, and for whom. He watched hundreds of kinds of flowers for years. He saw that coloured lines on petals point to the nectar. He saw that in many flowers the pollen is ripe before the stigma is ready. Such a flower cannot use its own pollen. Insects had to be carrying it across. In 1793 he published a book with careful drawings of about 500 kinds of flowers. Hardly anybody believed him, and the next year he lost his post at the school. In 1862 Charles Darwin, who had read the book, published his own tests on orchids. He wrote that Sprengel had been right.
how_we_found_out.who: Christian Konrad Sprengel, a German schoolteacher (1750 to 1816), and later Charles Darwin
how_we_found_out.when: Sprengel made his first observation in 1787 and published his book in 1793. Darwin's book on orchids came out in 1862.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a flower pollinates itself, and that insects only steal nectar. Sprengel showed that in many flowers the pollen and the stigma are ready at different times. So the pollen must come from another flower, and insects carry it.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in old-fashioned clothes kneeling in a meadow at dawn, looking closely at a wild geranium flower with a small bee on it, a sketchbook open beside him.
how_we_found_out.context: Do flowers pollinate themselves, and what are insects really doing on them? This card tells the true story of a schoolteacher in Germany who looked closely at flowers.

roots.context: In the Hairy or Smooth test you carried haldi from box to box on a cotton bud. In the Clean-up Count you watched ants clear crumbs from your floor. Here we ask who makes a fruit, when a plant and an insect both have a part in it.

deep_truth.truth: In the Hairy or Smooth test, the cotton bud left haldi on far more boxes than the pen. A bee is covered in hairs, and she visits flowers to collect food for her colony. Pollen clings to her hairs and rubs off on the next flower. So many fruits begin with a few grains of pollen that an insect spilled while collecting food.
deep_truth.habit: We say that a tree makes fruit, and we call an insect a helper or a pest. We speak as though each lived a separate life. A mango needs the tree and also an insect who was busy feeding herself or her family.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Hairy or Smooth test, the cotton bud went on leaving haldi for many boxes after one dip. In the Raisin at the Bottom, the hand that only fetched raisins left haldi on the second flower's collar. About three out of four main food crops gain from animal pollinators.

three.who_am_i: Much of your body was built from foods that an insect pollinated. You are also a kind of colony: billions of living cells that share one body.
three.what_is_life: Living beings feed on each other and pass material on. A dead moth becomes young ants, and a fallen leaf becomes soil for a new plant.
three.what_is_this_world: Pollinating and recycling go on around you every day. Nobody orders this work and nobody pays for it, and all our food depends on it.

roots.thread: A flower cannot walk to another flower, and a bee cannot make sugar from sunlight. Each has what the other lacks. Flowers and insects have lived together for more than 100 million years, and each has shaped the other's body. Many wise teachers taught that all beings share one life in many forms. This lesson shows a similar idea in a practical way. A mango is made by a tree, a fly and the recyclers in the soil, all working together.

teachings.teaching: This part of the text is called the honey teaching. It says: this earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth.
teachings.link: The Sanskrit word is madhu, which means honey. The teaching says that each thing feeds the others and is fed by them. A flower feeds a bee, and the bee's visit starts the flower's seeds.

teachings.teaching: A bee takes nectar from a flower and flies away without harming the flower's colour or scent. A wise person should go through a village in the same way.
teachings.link: The verse holds up the bee as someone who takes without harming. This lesson adds something the verse does not say: the flower gains from the visit.

teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper, and you can see the cloud, the rain and the tree in it. He called this interbeing.
teachings.link: Look at a mango in the same way. The fly who carried the pollen is in the mango. So is the dead fish that fed the fly when she was young.

science.text: Nearly nine in ten kinds of flowering plant are pollinated by animals, and most of those animals are insects.
Some scientists call an ant or bee colony a superorganism, one living body made of many animals. Others say this hides the fact that each insect senses and chooses for herself.

other_view.who: Many biologists who study flowers and their visitors
other_view.view: A flower and a bee are not partners who look after each other. Each takes as much as possible and gives as little as possible. Carpenter bees often bite a hole in the side of a flower and drink the nectar without touching the pollen. Some orchids offer no nectar at all and are still visited. On this view pollination is a bargain with cheating on both sides, and words like 'helping' mislead us.

playtest: This lesson was read through step by step, as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. It has not yet been done at home. The Hairy or Smooth test (core) needs haldi, two cotton buds, a plastic pen, white paper and a ruler. It takes about 30 minutes. The expected result is that the cotton bud marks 8 to 15 boxes. The dry pen end marks 1 to 4. The pen must be dry: a damp or oily pen picks up a thick coat of haldi and marks many boxes. Haldi stains cloth, so work on newspaper. The Clean-up Count (core) needs ants. Small house ants are present in most Indian homes, but not in every home on every day. The steps say to try a balcony, a doorstep or the foot of a tree. They also say to move the paper closer if no ant comes in 15 minutes. Some kinds of ant feed at the paper and carry little away. Then the count of ants is the main result. The counting takes about 10 minutes spread over 40, so use the gaps for the cards or the story. The Kitchen Shelf Test works with whatever foods are in the kitchen. A missing food can be a name on a slip of paper. The Raisin at the Bottom needs a grown-up to tape the cotton buds. They must lean in over the tumbler. Jumping Pollen depends on dry air, and it often fails on a damp monsoon day. The step says so. A Flower Calendar for Our Street needs no garden. It does need one older person who knows the local trees. The Buzz Flower works best with haldi and atta mixed. The mixed powder clumps and stays in until the tube is shaken. If the powder pours out of the still tube, the hole is too big. Facts to treat with care: a worker's summer life of about six weeks is the usual figure for the European honeybee. So is a queen's 1,000 or more eggs a day. Indian hive bees have smaller colonies. The figures of 100 flowers a trip and 10 trips a day in the maths are rough. The share of flies among visitors to mango flowers differs from orchard to orchard. The 28-year-old ant queen was a black garden ant kept in a laboratory in Europe. The count of flying insects in Germany comes from one long study. The unit says that India has few such counts. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad and Dhammapada lines are given as paraphrases.
